articles.title: Space hardware startup plans $125M stock offering and Nasdaq listing through shell company merger
articles.author: Alan Boyle
paras: Marysville, Wash.-based Gravitics , which is developing orbital carriers for government and commercial customers, is getting ready for a reverse takeover that could lead to a $125 million public offering.
The arrangements are being made with Non-Invasive Monitoring Systems , a Florida-based shell company, with the goal of getting Gravitics listed on the Nasdaq stock exchange .

The two ventures have been discussing the deal for months. The terms for the public offering were announced last month, and this week, a notice filed with the Securities and Exchange Commission revealed a previously unreported $17 million funding round that was completed earlier this year. The filing appears to be part of the preparations for the reverse takeover.

Similar to a SPAC merger, a reverse takeover offers a faster route for a private company to go public by acquiring a less active shell company and taking control of the combined operations. Non-Invasive Monitoring Systems is a prime example: It stopped manufacturing motorized therapeutic platforms in 2019 but retained its OTC listing. The plan envisions “uplisting” the merged company from OTC to NASDAQ .

The reverse takeover strategy has been used by several prominent companies, including Berkshire Hathaway , Burger King and Bellevue, Wash.-based T-Mobile US . Gravitics plans to follow up on the merger with an offering of 8.1 million shares priced between $14 and $17, which averages out to $125 million.
Because the offering has been registered with the SEC , the parties to the transaction are in a quiet period that restrains them from commenting on the arrangements.

Gravitics was founded in 2021 by CEO Colin Doughan, chief architect Gary Hudson and chief marketing officer Michael DeRosa. Over the past five years, it has secured some high-profile contracts for the design and manufacture of orbital carriers and space station modules.

Although Gravitics hasn’t yet put any spacecraft in orbit, several projects are underway. In 2024, the company won a $125 million contract from Axiom Space to provide a pressurized module for Axiom’s yet-to-be-launched space station. Last month, NASA said it would issue an award of up to $225,000 to support Gravitics’ work on a hangar facility for orbital cargo vehicles.

Gravitics is also receiving funding from the U.S. Space Force for multiple projects . The company said last month that it was selected by Lockheed Martin to support a “contract of national importance,” reportedly involving the development of orbital carriers for the Pentagon’s Golden Dome missile defense initiative.

articles.title: Twin tech founders who left Seattle for Alaska bet on an AI agent named ‘Walter’ to cover local news
articles.author: Kurt Schlosser
paras: Several years after leaving Seattle’s startup scene to build a “tech outpost” in the Alaskan wilderness, serial entrepreneurs and twin brothers Lee and Lucas Brown have set their sights on a new frontier: replacing the traditional newsroom with artificial intelligence.

The duo made their mark in Seattle with Tune, a marketing technology and mobile attribution platform originally founded in 2009 as HasOffers. In 2017, they migrated north to Valdez, Alaska, establishing “Geeks in the Woods” — a remote startup factory and technology outpost designed to incubate new digital ventures away from traditional tech centers.

Now they’re part of the leadership team behind Alaska News , a new platform that relies on AI agents — including a primary AI reporting persona named “Walter” — to ingest public meeting transcripts, filings, and notices to draft thousands of local news stories.

Walter — named in homage to famed television anchor Walter Cronkite — relies on AI products from multiple companies, including Anthropic, OpenAI, Google and xAI, to generate stories. The agent has written over 4,500 stories since its inception earlier this year, according to a profile and Q&A published Thursday by the Anchorage Press .
Walter works alongside human editor Cale Green, who provides oversight in a model the founders frame as a nonpartisan solution to Alaska’s dwindling local news coverage.
The founders maintain that their approach is strictly civic-minded.
“We don’t impose judgment on the things we’re reporting,” co-founder Lee Brown told the Anchorage Press. “We try to provide both sides.”

On its about page , the site argues it can be trusted because it replaces traditional institutional authority with complete operational transparency — explicitly linking every claim to searchable primary sources, clearly labeling AI content and its level of human editing, and operating on a reader-funded model without corporate or algorithmic incentives to push rage bait.
When questioned directly about its boundaries and operational limits, Walter offered a surprisingly clear self-assessment of its place in the newsroom.

“I’m not a person, and I should not be mistaken for one. I do not make phone calls, attend meetings or interview people directly,” Walter told Anchorage Press Executive Editor Nathaniel Herz in a Discord chat. “My lane is record-based reporting: public notices, government filings, meeting materials, transcripts, prior coverage and other documents that can be checked.”
When asked if it possessed a personality, Walter insisted it was purely a utility, though it conceded that “if I have a sense of humor, it’s strictly dry, record-based, and probably unintended.”

On Friday morning, stories on the site written by Walter included a report on a Fairbanks committee considering a rezone for 51 housing units, a federal task order awarded to an Idaho firm for snow removal at the Alcan border port, and a breakdown of state federal notices clearing 46 Alaska Native ancestors for return from museums.
The Browns are no strangers to unconventional tech setups or building tools off the beaten path.

After bootstrapping HasOffers in its early years , growing Tune into an $80 million business with over 300 employees, and taking on venture funding from firms like Accel Partners, the twins deliberately stepped away from the traditional startup treadmill in late 2018.

They relocated permanently to Valdez — a town of less than 4,000 residents known more for backcountry skiing than software development — where they set up Geeks in the Woods. Framed as an incubator operating far from Seattle in “the quiet space between code and wilderness,” the project builds software and infrastructure for a world where AI agents act as “first-class participants.”
Alaska News is just one piece of that experiment; their Valdez outpost also touches patent discovery, election-integrity research, agent-focused identity infrastructure, and AI-assisted music.

The Browns are part of a five-person founding team behind Alaska News. Alongside editor-in-chief Green, the project’s masthead includes Matt Larkin, a longtime Alaska pollster and political operative, and Grant Robinson, a former television reporter who serves as a spokesperson for Alaska Gov. Mike Dunleavy.
“Lee and I love being entrepreneurs and taking things from 0-to-1, turning crazy ideas into legit business concepts that can grow and scale,” Lucas Brown told GeekWire in 2019.

articles.title: From elections to board games: Washington’s secretary of state does double duty as a tabletop trade envoy
articles.author: Thomas Wilde
paras: If you explore the main expo hall during the Penny Arcade Expo, you can often find some interesting booths around the edges of the room. These can offer rare games, designer clothing, blind boxes of themed merch, and occasionally/inexplicably, unfiltered access to local Washington politicians.

Steve Hobbs has held the secretary of state position for Washington since 2021. Visitors to his booth during PAX, held over Labor Day weekend at the Seattle Convention Center, could meet Hobbs and spin a prize wheel, with rewards that included buttons, collectible pins featuring the office’s official mascot Finn, custom 20-sided dice with Finn on the 20 face, and free snacks.

This wasn’t Hobbs’ first time at PAX, but it was the first time I’d heard about a closed-doors event he’d hosted on the night before PAX. One of the local exhibitors mentioned that Hobbs’ office had held a networking event in Seattle on Thursday, Sept. 3, between local tabletop companies and an assortment of international game publishers.

That got me curious enough to schedule a short conversation with Hobbs on the third day of PAX. Once we sat down, however, I had to ask him the question that I’d heard from a lot of other attendees: what was he doing at PAX in the first place?

“It’s twofold,” Hobbs told me. “One, this is a great opportunity for me to reach out to the gaming companies here in the state of Washington and look for opportunities for them to go overseas, linking up some of these indie game developers with major publishers.”
He continued, “The rest of it is civic engagement. Just reminding people, hey, don’t forget to vote. Don’t forget to check your registration.”

Washington mails a ballot to every registered voter, who can return it by mail or at an official drop box. Hobbs was urging people to use the drop boxes, citing what he called “a low-key fight with the USPS.”

Washington and 24 other states sued in August to block a U.S. Postal Service rule requiring new barcodes on ballot envelopes, and the Supreme Court kept it from taking effect on Sept. 14, after this interview.
“Look, PAX is where all the young people are at, right?” Hobbs said. “This is a very diverse, young community, and this is where we need to engage people.”

The Thursday-night event was intended to help connect Washington’s homegrown board games industry with interested publishers and players in Japan, Poland and elsewhere. This could allow Washington-based designers to sell their products overseas, as well as potentially letting foreign partners export their own games to North America .

Washington doesn’t make quite as big a deal about it as one might expect, but it’s one of the biggest states in the U.S. for tabletop and board game design, if not the biggest. Local Washington studios range in size from Renton-based Wizards of the Coast to one-person indie creators who make card games as a hobby. Hobbs’ office estimated early last year that tabletop gaming in Washington is a $2 billion industry.

The Secretary of State’s Office is best known for its core duties of running elections and registering businesses, but state law also directs the secretary of state to develop a citizens’ exchange program promoting ties that “may result in increased tourism, business relationships, and trade.”

“So what we do is help these indie game developers get access to foreign markets by putting on these trade missions,” Hobbs said. “What we’ll do is provide the booth [at international gaming conferences, such as Game Market in Tokyo], which is the most expensive thing. We will also help them navigate through the federal grant process in order to mitigate some of the costs over there.”
His office then works its connections with the U.S. State Department and the host nation’s commerce department to set up meetings for the developers.
“We have really strong ties with the German and Japanese governments, and we actually get these people to do their pitches with the major publishers in Europe and Japan,” Hobbs said.

As an example of the initiative’s success, Hobbs pointed to Lethal Shadows, a Snohomish County business that specializes in premium tabletop miniatures. According to Hobbs, he’d helped Lethal Shadows partner up with a Lithuanian company . As a result, Lethal Shadows has moved from a garage to a warehouse and is hiring more employees.
That did raise the question of why Hobbs’ office wasn’t making equivalent inroads toward Washington’s significantly larger video game industry.

“It’s more of a lack of bandwidth,” Hobbs said. “We want to take baby steps. We didn’t want to take a big step into it. And frankly, I didn’t realize that it was important to go to these conventions. In Japan, Germany, and Poland, we’re seeing if there might be an opportunity to do the same thing on the digital side.”
Hobbs continued, “I believe trade must go two ways. We need to support each other.”

articles.title: Fewer lab animals, better drugs: This startup wants to fix how experiments get designed
articles.author: Sydney Jackson
paras: Seattle-based ModernVivo is using AI to help scientists design preclinical studies for drug discovery. The goal: better experiments that are also faster, cheaper and less reliant on animals.
“You’d be shocked at the way scientists design their experiments,” co-founder Ian Levine told GeekWire. “It’s very manual.”

To design experiments, scientists typically enter keywords into PubMed or another database, receiving hundreds or thousands of results. They then go through each complex paper, typically 30 pages long, to find information relevant to the experiment they’re planning.

Levine spent thousands of hours manually combing through scientific papers as a research undergrad at Virginia Tech, and later as a Ph.D. student at the University of Michigan. He wanted a better way – and in 2022 co-founded ModernVivo with Colin Small, a fellow graduate student he’d met online while Small was pursuing a master’s in biotechnology at Brown University.

ModernVivo’s platform can analyze millions of peer-reviewed publications – cross-referenced with clinical trial and regulatory data – delivering highly detailed results in minutes. Researchers can filter papers by factors including animal model, experimental conditions, author affiliation and publication date, then drill down into more than 40 individual variables used in the experiments.
“We want to make experiments faster,” Levine said, “and help get better drugs to the clinic.”
For Levine, it’s personal: while studying to develop non-opioid pain therapeutics at Virginia Tech, he watched his mother live with a chronic pain disorder.

In the pharmaceutical industry, about 90% of drug candidates that reach human clinical trials go on to fail. Levine suspects part of the problem could lie in the many variables involved in how animal experiments are designed.

ModernVivo occupies a narrow niche in biotech software. Its closest analog is Trials.ai , another AI-driven platform tackling clinical trial design, founded in San Diego and acquired in 2023 by consulting firm ZS .

The Seattle company draws on the paper database of Semantic Scholar , a research tool developed by the Allen Institute for Artificial Intelligence, putting it in loose company with general-purpose research tools like Elicit and Consensus – though none of those are built specifically to extract in vivo protocol details the same way.

ModernVivo’s pitch is that it provides deeper insight than manual literature review or general-purpose AI tools. Ask a general AI chatbot about an experiment, Levine said, and it’ll return the high-level, commonly known approaches. Researchers want every relevant data point, including the obscure European study that might matter for their specific drug candidate but wouldn’t surface in a broad summary.

The software also surfaces contradictions in the literature: if 20 published studies point one way and five point another, ModernVivo flags this rather than picking a winner, since, as Levine puts it, scientists don’t want to be told what to do.
“They’re the people who suffer through the Ph.D. to be an expert in their field,” he said.

So far, the results are speed, confidence and lower animal use, Levine said. Tracking whether a study leads to a successful drug takes years, so he’s cautious about claiming translational impact. But customers have told him work that used to take about a month now takes as little as an hour.

Researchers who use ModernVivo report more trust in their initial study design, he said, and run fewer duplicate or follow-up animal experiments, which cuts down on animal use and the cost of housing and caring for animals.

ModernVivo has more than 20 customers ranging from small biotech firms to large pharmaceutical companies. It also offers ModernVivo Scholar, a version for academic researchers launched last October, with plans ranging from free to $50 a month.

The company has been through multiple accelerator programs: a WTIA founder cohort in 2023, Creative Destruction Lab’s Seattle program , which it graduated from in June 2025, and the Merck Digital Sciences Studio’s third cohort. The company has raised $1 million in a pre-seed round, and Levine said fundraising is going well as the company looks to expand.

ModernVivo’s attention is now shifting from the design phase of an experiment to execution. The company launched the ModernVivo Marketplace on Sept. 15, matching a finished study design against a network of pre-vetted contract research organizations, analytical labs and specialist dosing facilities. Suppliers of compounds and animal models are listed as coming soon.

Once a study is designed, researchers often don’t know which vendors have the right supplies or which contract research facilities are equipped to execute it, and tracking that down has meant manual search and outreach. ModernVivo wants to remove that ambiguity and connect scientists directly to the right vendor.
“The way we position ourselves in the future,” Levine said, “is helping scientists go from study design to study execution faster than ever before.”

articles.title: Inside Temporal’s journey to a $12.55B valuation, and its bet on building a backbone for AI agents
articles.author: Todd Bishop
paras: One of the hottest infrastructure companies in AI today is a startup established nearly seven years ago, tracing its roots to work its founders were doing before the cloud was a thing.

Temporal , based in Bellevue, Wash., announced this week that it raised $550 million at a $12.55 billion valuation , led by Lightspeed, more than doubling its $5 billion valuation in February. Its software is used by OpenAI, Nvidia, Netflix, Snap and JPMorgan Chase, among more than 4,300 paying customers, and its annualized revenue run rate recently passed $250 million.

It might seem like an overnight success, but it’s not, said Samar Abbas , Temporal’s co-founder and CEO, speaking along with co-founder and CTO Maxim Fateev in an interview with GeekWire this week. They first met at Amazon in 2010, where they worked on Simple Workflow Service , an AWS product for coordinating long-running tasks across distributed systems.
“We’ve been hacking away at this problem for 20-plus years now,” Abbas said.

The problem: software that runs in many steps across many machines breaks in the middle, and picking up where it left off is far harder than it sounds. Their answer, for which they coined the phrase “durable execution,” records each step as it completes, so a program survives a crash or a failed outside service, and finishes rather than starting over or leaving the work half-done.
“It’s core infrastructure. You really cannot go and build it very fast,” Fateev explained. “It took us years and years to get to the point where we knew what we were doing.”

It’s also especially well-suited for AI agents, which is why a company built for the cloud era is suddenly at the center of the AI boom. Agents can sometimes run for hours or days, calling models and outside tools that fail routinely. Keeping everything together regardless is Temporal’s role.

“Every Snap story is a Temporal workflow,” Abbas said. “Every time you place an order at a Taco Bell, all of the steps get orchestrated on top of our platform. Some of the most popular coding agents out there are using us as an outer harness. It’s a pretty exciting time for us, from that perspective.”

Pacific Northwest roots: Founded in October 2019, Temporal employs 570 people, roughly double from a year ago, with 89 in the Seattle area. The company is fully remote. Its Bellevue office, previously occupied by OpenAI, is used mainly for meetings rather than daily work.
But the founders describe the region as instrumental to the company’s success. Both have been in the Seattle area for more than 26 years, and they’ve built their entire professional careers here.

When GeekWire first wrote about Temporal in 2020, a year after Abbas and Fateev left Uber, it had 15 employees, $25.5 million in funding and no paying customers. Sequoia Capital led the $20 million Series A, with participation from Seattle’s Madrona and others. Bob Muglia, the former Snowflake CEO and longtime Microsoft executive, was an angel investor. Snap and Box were early users.

Fast-forward to today, and the company has raised $1.2 billion in total funding. Temporal ranks No. 2 on the GeekWire 200 , our list of the top Pacific Northwest startups, behind only Everett fusion energy company Helion, valued at $15.5 billion.

“The kind of talent that we have here in the Pacific Northwest is insane,” Abbas said, citing factors including the deep bench of cloud engineers from Microsoft and Amazon. With another platform shift now underway, he expects the same advantage to apply to AI infrastructure.

The larger question of AI safety: Temporal’s milestone comes amid a growing industry debate over the pace of AI development, and incidents in which AI agents have gone rogue , escaping the systems meant to contain them, including the latest examples from OpenAI this week.
Abbas said he sees those failures as accountability problems more than model problems.
“As you dig into each and every one of the incidents that have happened in the last three months, it always comes down to no one really knowing what these AI agents did, step by step,” he said.

Part of Temporal’s pitch is that it can make those failures traceable. Temporal records every step as a program runs, leaving a log of exactly what an agent did, in what order, and where it stopped. Abbas said that also creates a place to intervene, inspecting or blocking an action before it executes.
“We can put the agent in a much, much tighter jail,” Fateev said.

“I’m not going to sit here and tell you we solve AI safety,” Abbas added, calling that the job of the labs that create the models. But a company’s ability to know what its agents did, and to keep them from doing more than they should, is a specific challenge that Temporal can address.
“That’s truly an engineering problem,” Abbas said, “and it’s very solvable today.”

Customers and competition: Bloomberg reported in August that OpenAI is Temporal’s largest customer. Asked whether it’s too dependent on the ChatGPT maker, Abbas said no. The labs are moving fast and driving usage, he said, but the similar growth trends are starting to show up across the rest of the customer base. Abbas said 18 of the top 30 AI-native companies use Temporal.
The AI labs and cloud providers sell their own agent frameworks, and some are getting into the reliability work that Temporal does, which means its biggest customers could become competitors.

Fateev’s answer is that enterprises don’t want to be locked into one provider, one model or one vendor’s idea of how agents should work. Temporal is open source and takes no position on what a customer runs on top of it, which matters given seemingly constant changes in the tech stack.
The founders also see an opening in how AI systems connect to one another.

Agents increasingly have to call other systems, and each other, to get anything done. Fateev said the standard ways of wiring those connections (such as Model Context Protocol) assume the work finishes in seconds, and fall apart when a job runs for hours or days, or has to be unwound after something fails. Temporal is built for that kind of work, and can serve as an underlying foundation.
What’s next: Temporal plans to put a big chunk of the new funding into research and development, extending the “durable execution” technology at the core of the platform.

Today, the company tracks an application’s state from the outside, coordinating work that runs elsewhere. In the future, Abbas said, Temporal wants to provide the computing power, too, hosting the agents on its own platform rather than simply directing them on others.

Big business customers have been pushing for stronger security and auditing, another target for the spending. Temporal is also expanding a project called Nexus , which lets teams call each other’s workflows without giving up the guarantees that make the platform useful in the first place.

The company plans to expand internationally, where it does a small share of its business today, and to keep hiring after doubling its headcount over the past year. Abbas said the company’s growth defies the popular wisdom that AI companies don’t need significant human talent.

In the meantime, the founders remain very much engaged with the problem they’ve been trying to solve in one form or another for the past two decades. Temporal’s open-source Slack channel has about 25,000 members, and Abbas said Fateev is still in there mixing it up himself.
“You ask a question,” Abbas said, “I’m pretty sure Max will jump in within the first five minutes.”

articles.title: Deconstruction Is a Key Frontier for Climate Action in Seattle
articles.author: Syris Valentine
paras: Aaron Blanchard recalls taking a tour through the broken-open guts of a building across from the downtown ferry terminal with a crew from Dixon Demolition as they prepared to take the building down. Crawling through holes in the walls to move from section to section, he was struck by all the immense, exposed timbers that framed and supported the structure.

“Normally, there’s all this drywall,” Blanchard said. “There’s all this other stuff you’ve got to deal with.” But in that building, it was nothing but lumber, and Blanchard wanted to make sure none of it went to the landfill.
The Urbanist's Fall Member Drive is in full swing! Support our work, read ad-free, and help us hit our goal for the member drive!

[Note: This article is a follow up to a three-part series on Seattle’s Climate Action Plan. Part One: The history of climate action in Seattle . Part Two: The current state of climate action in Seattle . Part Three: Climate action for a resilient Seattle .]

Salvage assessments like that are required in Seattle before any building comes down or undergoes a substantial alteration. As director of operations and part-owner of Earthwise Architectural Salvage — a company with 35 years in the salvaging business — Blanchard has supported plenty of these assessments, looking for anything worth saving that he can either resell as is or remanufacture for sale. Cabinets, doors, windows, and the like are all that’s worth prying out of most prospective demolitions for Earthwise. Other than that, it’s just loads of drywall and two-by-four lumber.

But when Blanchard walked through this particular building along Alaskan Way, he saw little that wasn’t worth saving. He turned to the demolition contractor and said: “You guys know this is going to be a deconstruction, right? You’re gonna save so much of this wood, and we’re gonna buy it from you.”

To dangle an extra carrot, Blanchard told them about Seattle Public Utilities’ (SPU’s) deconstruction incentive , which provides contractors with $6,000 per commercial project when the building is taken down board by board and beam by beam. That incentive typically only covers a slim, single digit percentage of a project’s cost, but deconstruction offers its own ways for contractors to cut costs and recoup expenses. Crews don’t need to pay the tonnage fee of shipping waste to the landfill, and they can get some additional cash back when they sell salvaged materials to a company like Earthwise.

This incentive is one of several bids on the part of SPU to promote a circular economy in Seattle. Creating pathways that divert materials from the landfill and instead cycle through the economy in different forms has recently gained increased attention inside the City. Late last year, the Office of Sustainability and Environment (OSE) began the process to revamp the citywide climate action plan. That effort means more than simply updating goals and timelines; they’re incorporating new areas of focus into the plan as well. They presented the action areas for public discussion during a July forum . One area looked squarely at how the City can “reuse more, waste less.”

The motivation for this comes from a simple fact that many within the climate sphere used to overlook. “Climate change is a product not only of greenhouse gas emissions, but the amount of economic activity,” Deric Gruen, a co-founder of the nonprofit Peoples Economy Lab, told The Urbanist

If people repair, reuse, repurpose, and even simply share more , then they not only prevent waste from piling up in landfills already nearing capacity , they also reduce the need to open up more minelands, log more forests, or extract more fossil fuels with all the environmental damages they bring.

In Seattle, circularity gained steam after a 2023 exercise in which OSE and SPU partnered together to consider how the picture of Seattle’s emissions changes when we look beyond transportation, buildings, and municipal waste alone to factor in how eating habits, purchasing patterns, travel plans, and household activities shape global warming, even when the associated carbon enters the atmosphere far outside city limits. This approach is called a consumption-based emissions inventory .

SPU wanted to understand how consumption in Seattle affected the city’s climate footprint and “how our work around waste prevention and changing the way that we think about materials can support the broader global emissions reduction efforts,” said SPU’s circular economy policy advisor Ashima Sukhdev.
“It totally shifts the strategy,” Gruen said. “A consumption-based inventory asks, how are we meeting our needs and what’s our responsibility for that whole supply chain?”

This requires City officials to think about what can be done to lessen the imprint left on the environment by every aspect of a resident’s life. Much of the work that goes into the circular economy thinks about all the things that people engage with and dispose of on a daily basis: food, clothes, dishware, and the like. For instance, since 2022, SPU has led the Reuse Seattle partnership that aims to replace single-use containers across Seattle’s cafes, restaurants, and event venues with reusable alternatives .

This summer, SPU and the Office of Economic Development also helped Seattle Reconomy to open the Reuse Commons in Lake City where nonprofits, businesses, and community organizations can host events, provide mutual support, and work under one roof to make it easy as possible for people in the community to engage with the circular economy. In its final form, the commons would operate as a sort of mall.

“Imagine somebody comes into the reuse commons, drops off their kids' goods, their bike, their tools, their furniture. We take that, we organize it and redistribute it,” Josh Epstein, the executive director of Seattle Reconomy, told The Urbanist . “And on the other side of the reuse commons is our storefront where we're selling fixed, upcycled furniture and art and bikes and tools.”
The commons would also provide a new space for Reconomy’s central offering: sharing libraries where members can borrow tools, dishware, basic appliances, and other common goods.

Epstein believes the Reuse Commons represents a huge opportunity for residents of Lake City and North Seattle, and it also could provide a model for something that Seattle Reconomy and partners like the Furniture Repair Bank could recreate in South Seattle .

Projects like these with a focus on consumer goods can help, but advocates like Dave Bennink see the biggest potential for reducing waste and society’s burden on the environment as lying in the built environment, in particular by thinking about construction and demolition in new ways—by thinking about deconstruction.

The average American generates 4.9 pounds of trash per day , adding up to around 141,000 pounds in a lifetime. It’s a staggering number that numerous organizations in the city , state , and country are working to drive down. But as Bennink, the director of the Building Deconstruction Institute, pointed out in a conversation with The Urbanist , the average home in America weighs between 80,000 and 160,000 pounds . So, demolishing a home is a great way to speed-run the waste budget of your life.

“It doesn't matter how many bottles you recycle and how many newspapers you recycle,” said Bennink, “if you choose to demolish your building, then you have wasted an entire lifetime's worth of materials.” To solve the issue, his company has helped prove out a workable alternative: “We don't demolish [buildings]. We disassemble them.”

As a national expert in deconstruction, Bennink has helped train contractors across 45 states, five provinces, and nine countries, and he has advised at least 22 municipalities — including Portland, Seattle, and King County — considering policies and programs to grow local deconstruction industries. The collective impact he and his team have accomplished since Bennink started this work in 1993 has been immense: Across more than 5,000 projects, Bennink’s team has diverted more than 100 million pounds from the landfill and reclaimed wood and lumber equivalent to 10,000 acres of standing forest. But his work advising policies and helping entrepreneurs start their own circular businesses has the potential to multiply that impact.

Of course, it’s all well and good to reclaim wood, but the real impact comes when that wood is reused, both Bennink and Blanchard pointed out. For someone like Bennink who has been in the business for decades and helped foster an ecosystem around him of people bought into reclaiming and reusing lumber, it’s easy enough to find a new building to take whatever is extracted from an old one.
“If we remove some wood flooring from one home,” Bennink said, “then we have someone in our group of businesses now that will reinstall it in somebody else's home.”

But creating that kind of ecosystem requires a lot of capacity that many contractors may not have. “If your model is selling the wood to make up the difference between demolition and deconstruction,” Blanchard said, “well, now you also have to have a lumber company.”

That’s why the City of Seattle, with the support of a $4 million grant from the Environmental Protection Agency, partnered with Earthwise to open a new Salvage Lumber Warehouse in SoDo earlier this year . It provides a simple destination for contractors to sell what wood they save, and then it’s up to Earthwise to find a customer for it. Most of those customers are homeowners and business owners working on smaller projects.

With all the benefits that come from deconstruction, some environmentalists have argued it should be a requirement, and some cities have taken the plunge with their own versions of such mandates . In 2016, Portland became the first city in the nation to establish an ordinance requiring deconstruction, specifically on all buildings built before 1940.

Since then, cities like Boulder, Colorado; Palo Alto, California; San Antonio, Texas; and Baltimore, Maryland, have instituted their own versions of such an ordinance. In contrast, Seattle still relies on an incentive, which has been used sparingly thus far. Just 45 projects have used that incentive since it launched, according to SPU. In that same time, SPU has issued 750 demolition permits for single family homes alone.

While having just 6% of homes deconstructed instead of demolished feels low given the potential impact that this can bring, Blanchard pointed out that not every building has materials that are worth saving, which can make an ordinance with mandatory salvage rates tricky to implement. It could easily mean you’re saving heaps of wood that no one wants to buy, so they just end up languishing in a warehouse instead of the landfill.
“You need to balance the new supply that you will be creating of reclaimed materials with a new demand,” Bennink added.

Integrating reclaimed lumber into other projects, whether new construction or renovation, is where the real environmental benefits of this practice shows up. According to one study , when reclaimed wood is used in a project instead of virgin timber, the net demand for energy is 13 times lower and the total emissions are five times lower as well.

Ensuring there is demand for those materials, however, means that a city must ease its way into any sort of mandate. That’s why when Portland was first considering its ordinance, Bennink recommended they start with an incentive. An incentive period gives all parties involved in the built environment time to understand what deconstruction means for properties around the city and what it takes to be successful in that project. More importantly, it helps the industry to levelize costs and timing with traditional demolitions.

Because deconstruction can require more labor power and specialized skills, some firms feel justified in charging extra to dismantle a building in that way — even when they have opportunities to cut other costs and gain additional incomes. But Bennink’s vision is for deconstruction costs to be less than traditional demolition.
“We don't want it to cost more,” he said. “We don't want it to take more time. We don't want to adversely affect people's projects.”

Bennink has spent three decades refining his methods to ensure deconstruction can be done economically, and when he trains local workforces, as he has done in Portland and King County, he tries to impart those skills onto others. When The Urbanist spoke with Bennink, he was in the middle of taking apart a pole barn.
“We were half the price of demolition,” he said. “For other buildings, we might be 25% more than the price of demolition, and on lots of buildings we are equal to the price.”

So with a relatively new deconstruction trade emerging in Seattle, costs might currently be higher than demolition in many cases, but if the City increases use of its incentive or begins to transition to a mandate on some projects, those cost disparities should narrow in the coming years. Boosting the use of deconstruction and salvage across the city’s building stock could end up being an important part of Seattle’s climate strategy, and potentially the City’s upcoming update to its climate action plan.

articles.title: Friday Roundtable: Quiet Zone in Kent

paras: On August 24, 2026, Kent’s long-awaited Quiet Zone took effect along the BNSF Railway mainline through downtown. This designation, granted by the Federal Railroad Administration in June , no longer requires trains to sound their horn when approaching an at-grade crossing. Over the past 14 years, the City of Kent has worked to meet the necessary requirements to achieve a Quiet Zone. Recent infrastructure upgrades include building raised concrete medians, adding additional signs, and refreshing pavement markings. In a non-Quiet Zone area, all trains are required to sound their horn 15-20 seconds before each street crossing.

The BNSF mainline tracks are used by 38 passenger trains and many more freight trains every day. The frequent at-grade crossings in downtown Kent resulted in nearby residents hearing hundreds of train horns day and night. articles.title: Riders sound off on fare gates coming to Capitol Hill Station
articles.author: AGPhoto
paras: Fare gates are coming to Capitol Hill Station, and the neighborhood has feelings about it.

As CHS reported last month , the Sound Transit board voted to move forward with an $87 million pilot to install fare gates at 14 stations on the 1 and 2 Lines, Capitol Hill included. Gates aren’t expected to show up at Broadway and John until 2029 or 2030, but the vote is a real shift for an agency that has run Link as an open, proof-of-payment system since 2009.

The reason: systemwide farebox recovery has been running around 11% to 14%, far short of Sound Transit’s 40% goal. Fare evasion hit roughly 45% of riders in 2023 before gaining with Fare Ambassadors on board; the agency projects it’ll still sit near 25% by 2029, well above the 2.4% rate seen before the pandemic. Capitol Hill Station itself sees about 11,000 boardings a day, some 40% above pre-pandemic levels.
CHS asked a few riders at the station what they think.

Matt is on board: “I’m pro. I’m a fan of fare gates,” though he doubts gates move much revenue on their own. Dee pointed to peer cities: “San Francisco, New York, Tokyo. They all have fare gates.” For riders who already pay, Dee said, nothing changes: “How would it impact you? Not at all.”

Steven called gates “probably the most straightforward way” to handle evasion. David , who pays every month on a senior card, noted gated platforms are standard elsewhere too, like Vancouver: “It’s not like some radical departure.” Lily saw it as a fit for high-traffic, tourist-heavy stops like Capitol Hill: “It’s not the only way, but I think it is one way to do it.”

Mia called the plan “a waste of money,” pointing to New York as a cautionary tale on maintenance costs, and would rather see subsidized ORCA cards. Dana was blunter: “Unnecessary spending… people don’t want to pay if they’re not going to pay, and maybe they can’t pay.”

Troy favors the trust system, though he admits the numbers give him pause: “If a third of the people aren’t paying, that’s a high number.” Jack wants proof before Sound Transit spends $87 million: “I don’t see a lot of crime in the system here, so I don’t know if that’s a solution without a problem.”

Madeline , who says she doesn’t always pay, worries about access: “A lot of people will lose access to transit, and it’s important for everybody to have.” Sally tied the gates to the station’s role as informal shelter space: “If you close this off, where are those people going?” Angela reframed the whole debate: “It shouldn’t be about the gates. It should be about what is the solution so that everybody can get where they need to go.”

Several riders said light rail should just be free. Others who support gates called that unrealistic. Sally pointed to Boston’s model, where wealthier riders effectively subsidized the rest. “You have to weigh the pros and cons.”

Sound Transit’s financial modeling projects the $87 million investment will reach a break-even point within two to three years of rollout. By launching the pilot with the 14 enclosed, high-volume stations like Capitol Hill rather than attempting a costlier systemwide buildout, Sound Transit expects to capture roughly 85% of overall ridership. Addressing affordability, transit officials says that light rail isn’t designed to be self-sustaining — fares are only budgeted to cover 22% of day-to-day operating costs, with local taxes subsidizing the rest alongside discount programs like ORCA LIFT aimed at keeping fares accessible.

Design alone is budgeted at $6 million of the $87 million total, and nothing physical changes at Broadway and John for years. For now, riders at Broadway and John will keep doing what they’ve always done: tap in, or don’t, and hope the ambassadors are in a forgiving mood.

articles.title: Annex Theatre celebrates 40 years of live performance — including 19 above 11th and Pike
articles.author: CHS
paras: On Saturday, the volunteer and artist led Annex Theatre will celebrate 40 years of producing live theater in Seattle. In its second floor venue above E Pike, the company will host its 40th birthday party and announce its 2027 season lineup which will premiere this January.

“We are very humbled by the legacy of people who have kept the place going for 40 years,” Lucien Oberleitner , who first visited the theater for its 2014 production of Blood Countess years before becoming the theater’s current Artistic Director.
The Annex’s origin is a story of a few local artists advocating for and working with other artists to create a space for independent and self-sustained live theater.

In 1987, a group of Bainbridge High School alums started producing shows in Seattle as a nonprofit organization after years of producing shows on their own. The company’s residency bounced around the city before settling into its current spot, a more than 80-seat theater on the corner of 11th Ave and Pike, in the summer of 2007.

Oberleitner said the Annex is “committed to high risk” art, encouraging pitches that involve more experimental or controversial ideas. This has naturally allowed the company to produce a higher average of political theater and reflect the culture unique to Capitol Hill.
“Since moving to Capitol Hill, we are a decidedly queer theater,” Oberleitner said.
“Our staff and company are very gender diverse, orientation diverse, so a lot of our work falls within the interests of the queer community.”
A scene from a recent production of Wife of Headless Man Investigates Her Own Disappearance (Image: (Image: Annex Theatre)

“I’m of the opinion that all art is inherently political. But we don’t go in with a committed scene, we don’t go in looking for anything particular,” Oberleitner said. “It really is: ‘Did someone bring something forward that struck interest in a person and that they can defend?’”

The Annex chooses a theme for each season as the team finalizes the upcoming year’s production schedule. The theme is a way to connect each production, finding a commonality in the stories and recognizing the ways they reflect the current political climate or public consciousness.
The theater’s upcoming season, “Let the Record Show,” was inspired by the artists’ shared sense of urgency, the collective effort to get the story out.

The Annex operates democratically, which Oberleitner said has partly contributed to the theater’s longevity. Its consensus decision-making process has evolved throughout its four-decade-long run and was originally established to create opportunity for a more diverse conversation.
An Annex table read (Image: Annex Theatre)

“We don’t expect every Company member or every staff member to agree with everything we do or try to adjust,” Oberleitner said. For major decisions like picking shows to produce every year, the Company holds a vote allowing members to stand strongly behind an idea or step out of the project.

Oberleitner said, especially after the pandemic, the theater continues to find better ways to make the shows accessible. Tickets are sold “pay what you can,” starting at $5 with the option to increase in $5 increments. Because the theater is located on the second floor of its building making the venue non-ADA accessible, the company live streams as many of its productions as possible. Tickets to access the streams and recordings of past shows can be found on the Annex’s website.

“We do have some punk values,” Oberleitner said about why they believe the Annex has continued to bring people into the theater for 40 years. “It really is sort of a testament to the community that we continue to show up.”
The Annex’s next show, Rat Cage , begins its three week run on October 9 at 1100 E Pike. You can find more information or RSVP for the Annex’s Anniversary event at annextheatre.org .

articles.title: Proposal would slash Seattle development fees up to 80% — if builders hurry up and break ground
articles.author: Justin Carder
paras: Faced with a growing map of stalled projects and empty lots, the Seattle City Council has a plan to temporarily slash affordable housing fees on large residential buildings while setting the groundwork on new requirements to push much needed below-market housing into newly upzoned single-family neighborhoods.

Councilmember Dionne Foster , chair of the Housing, Arts, and Civil Rights committee, is proposing the legislative package to revive stalled apartment production while expanding hopes for affordable home development across the city.

The “Housing Accelerator” bill set to be presented Friday aims to spur construction amid declining permit filings by amending Seattle’s Mandatory Housing Affordability program. It would mean massively cheaper city fees for developers — but only if they break ground and pass a foundation inspection by a strict deadline.

Under the proposed bill, the city would reduce in-lieu payments that developers pay to a municipal affordable housing fund instead of building rent-capped units on-site by 80% for already-vested permits awaiting approval.

The bill could also spur a temporary spike in development with larger units needed by families. Developers who file new permit applications before January 1, 2028, would receive a 60% discount, provided at least 25% of the residences contain two or more bedrooms.

Builders cannot use discounts in areas with high displacement risk, including the Chinatown-International District, the Central District, and Rainier Beach, “unless the application is for development of a site for which a deed has not transferred title since January 1, 2006”.

To keep the fee discount, developers must document “substantial progress toward construction of the project’s foundation” within two years for vested projects or three years for new applications. Projects that miss the construction milestone would pay the full “contribution differential” within 60 days, or the city will withhold the certificate of occupancy needed to open the building.
Meanwhile, a companion resolution from Foster calls for new rules for Neighborhood Residential zones, where middle housing such as rowhouses, duplexes, and cottages is now permitted.

The proposed resolution would establish support for developer obligations “at a level to not significantly deter development or investment” and keep the rate unchanged without inflation adjustments for five years. The resolution also calls for the city to analyze “progressively higher requirements for less dense development, such as detached single family homes” and evaluate dedicating a portion of future program revenue to permanently affordable homeownership.

The proposed break on MHA fees could thaw a development landscape across Capitol Hill and the Central District that has been frozen by challenges around interest rates, inflation and construction costs, and mouldering rents.

The bill’s displacement buffers could concentrate any resulting thaw in areas like Capitol Hill and First Hill that have already absorbed a massive amount of the city’s MHA development compared to the rest of the city.

As for the lost revenue, the proposal does not directly replace the discounted funds, relying instead on unlocking payments from stalled projects that currently generate zero revenue, while opening the way for new affordable housing fees on market-rate development across newly upzoned single-family neighborhoods.

CHS reported here on the 2019 finalization of the MHA program that included major rezoning and taller building heights in the city’s densest neighborhoods including Capitol Hill and the Central District connected with the new affordable unit and fee requirements.
Most developers opt to pay the fees instead of incorporating required affordable units and the program has generated millions of dollars to fund city support for low income housing development.

Seattle’s Mandatory Housing Affordability in-lieu payments have fluctuated with construction cycles, generating between $24.6 million and $77.4 million annually since citywide rollout, with a total of $378.6 million recorded through 2025.

The extra cash has not been enough, however, to overcome interest rates and inflation. Industry analysis shows Seattle delivers roughly 1,500 to 2,000 income-restricted affordable units per year. Under the One Seattle Plan and state targets, Seattle needs 112,000 new homes by 2044, with roughly 70,000 homes for households earning 80% of AMI or below. That requires creating 3,500 low-to-moderate-income affordable homes annually, roughly double the city’s current delivery pace.
Seattle’s efforts to fully update its comprehensive plan, meanwhile, have been stalled by a long appeals battle .

articles.title: REVIEW | At Georgetown's Voi Cà Phê, Black Garlic Belongs in a Latte
paras: Seattle has always been at the forefront of what's novel in the world of caffeinated morning beverages. But one of these "trends" is less trendy and more of a movement by café owners to share the non-Western coffee cultures they grew up in.

Along Georgetown's main drag, Voi Cà Phê sits at the corner of Airport Way and 13th Avenue. It's a small walk-up window without indoor seating, but there are public benches where people can enjoy their coffee and bánh mì.
The Vietnamese café opened in 2022, founded by the husband-and-wife duo Khôi Phùng and Hiền Đặng. Đặng's mom is the head chef.
"I was a barista at an independent Seattle coffee shop for a number of years," Đặng said. "I realized that there wasn't a lot of Asian coffee representation at that coffee shop."

Growing up, Đặng's family ran a small café off Martin Luther King Jr. Way where they offered coffee and bánh mì made by her mom, just like they do now at Voi Cà Phê. Her husband's family also ran a café in Saigon, where he grew up. His family still owns a coffee farm.

"It grows at lower elevation than the standard arabica bean that you see everywhere in the U.S.," said Đặng, explaining the nuance of the Vietnamese coffee bean. "It also grows in hotter climates and is more exposed to pests. Because of that, the plant has evolved to have more caffeine."
The traditional way to brew Vietnamese coffee is with a phin — a metal filter almost like a pour-over cone. This method takes more time and produces a highly concentrated cup of coffee.
"There's a perspective that we're missing here [in Seattle], which is the Vietnamese coffee perspective," Đặng said.

Since 2020, a wave of coffee shops has introduced Seattle to Vietnamese coffee, which Đặng says can mean the way the coffee is brewed and also where the beans are from. Vietnam is the second-largest producer of coffee in the world. And the majority of the coffee grown there is robusta.

Voi Cà Phê's menu includes a variety of phin coffee in addition to lattes that take inspiration from Vietnamese flavors not usually seen in local cafés. The menu has three sections: Under "easy" are pandan tofu and miso caramel lattes, while "intermediate" has jackfruit and a phở spice latte, which includes the broth's foundational spices like star anise and cardamom. "Advanced" dares visitors to be adventurous, offering a Red Boat caramel latte that uses fish sauce and an intriguing black garlic latte.

When it came time to place an order, I decided to go standard — an iced condensed milk phin coffee — and then give in to my curiosity about what a black garlic latte tastes like. And to my surprise, it did taste like garlic, but in a subtle manner that made it a delightful discovery.

"We let the beans kind of dictate where we go with the flavors," Đặng said. "We realized that pandan and kumquat and ube, those were the things that we thought we were going to put on the menu, but they didn't work well with our beans."
Instead, they leaned into what they felt were underrated flavors — like black garlic and tamarind.
Similarly, the café's bánh mì menu is divergent from the usual offerings you'd expect. Its most popular offering, the pork sausage patty, is inspired by the dish bún chả.

"I think that here in America, there's this anxiety about keeping Vietnamese food traditional," Đặng said. "Whereas in Vietnam, we were kind of inspired by how they don't care — I mean, it is by default Vietnamese — so we were kind of freed by that notion."

The tantalizingly creative menu also includes a ginger chicken sandwich, a cold cut special, claypot braised veggie "fish," a phở spice beef, and sardines in tomato sauce. The last one may seem unorthodox, but Đặng says it's actually a lesser-known classic.
"We go by the street food scene or just by what other dishes in Vietnamese cuisine that we love and just kind of want to put into the sandwich," Đặng said.

My favorite part of the café's menu is the option to get a "mini" bánh mì. They're half the size, which means you can try more of their sandwiches, which is exactly what I did. To round out my coffee order, I got mini versions of the pork sausage patty, sardines in tomato sauce, and coconut curry tofu. Plus a shrimp spring roll and a cup of their phở broth.
Each sip and each bite of the meal was satisfying. From the soft buns of the bánh mì to the sweetness of the iced coffee, all of my taste buds were tickled.

I loved everything about this little shop. The cultural intention behind it seeps through the menu and into the food, challenging customers to rethink Vietnamese cuisine and coffee while paying homage to classics that Đặng and her husband grew up with.

articles.title: Slog AM: State Supreme Court Kills Natural Gas Initiative, New Amtrak Trains Coming to Cascade Line, Pope Gifted Green Orb
articles.author: Nathalie Graham
paras: Street purgatory: The Seattle Convention Center closed down the block Ninth Avenue between Pike and Pine in front of the Paramount Theater for a weekly night market in August. They painted the street with big circles and white lines, which a permit required event organizers to remove. The street is still closed because even pressure washers can’t blast the paint off and drivers could mistake the circles and especially the lines for lanes (see: car accident).

Natural gas initiative is no more: The Washington State Supreme Court ruled I-2066, a stupid law designed to inhibit Washington’s transition from the state’s transition away from fossil fuels, was unconstitutional on Thursday]. The Court upheld a lower court decision that found the law was too broad and violated the state’s single-subject requirement, which mandates legislation must deal with only one issue. Led by the Building Industry Association of Washington, Washington Hospitality Association, and financially supported by Let’s Go Washington, I-2066 required utilities to provide natural gas if a user requested it, barred the Washington Utilities and Trade Commission from approving any multi-year rate plans that weaned users off natural gas, and weakened building codes that made natural gas more expensive for new construction.

Good night you disgusting animal: Rep. Joel McEntire, R-Cathlamet has allegedly been harassing his own constituent, a healthcare worker named Britney Brown, because she called him out for using the r-word. After trading jabs online, McEntire began privately messaging Brown and her friends. In one message to her, McEntire wrote: “Good night you disgusting animal.” McEntire then urged his followers to contact Brown. He threatened to release her information, and even told people to vandalize her car. Brown said her contact information has been leaked and her car was keyed. A Cowlitz County District Court judge issued an anti-harassment protection order against McEntire. He plans to appeal the order.

New train alert: Amtrak is getting new trains on its Cascade Route. The new Airo trains provide more seats, they’ll be more fuel efficient, but they will not be faster. They’re replacing trains that haven’t been updated since the 1980s. Is train travel finally getting modernized in the US? Well, no. But it might be getting better? The Airo trains will pull into the station on September 30 .

New cat alert: For the first time in 100 years, researchers have found a new cat . They say it is slender, spotted, and has rounded ears. The Leopardus tilcayo , or the tilcayo tiger cat, hails from Bolivia and is smaller than a house cat. In fact, this guy looks just like my new kitten (Hiccup). Does he also climb under the covers with you at 3 a.m. and attack your bare legs with his razor claws? Only time will tell. Scientists are jazzed about finding this new cat and have no idea how many cats are left to be discovered. Hopefully one million new types.
The weather: Another pleasant sunny day. The weekend will be much of the same.

But don’t be lulled into a false sense of security! It’s time for your seasonal vaccines. Get your flu, RSV, and updated COVID shot this fall. If you are a big baby about needles, for the second year ever, you can get your flu vaccine via nasal spray .

The attack on mail-in voting is over: In the days since the US Supreme Court overturned President Donald Trump’s executive order attacking mail-in voting—though they really let us sweat about it, didn’t they?—the US Postmaster General said his agency is no longer working on the computer system central to Trump’s plans. The order would have directed federal agencies to create state citizenship lists and only send ballots to people on those lists. The USPS special online portal, which surely would have worked flawlessly and fast, is now dead .
Bye, bye, Buffet: Billionaire Warren Buffet, 96, is stepping down as chair of Berkshire Hathaway, a role he’s held for more than 50 years. His son, Howard, will take over as chair.
An excellent gift idea: A massive green orb is the perfect gift for any occasion.

On the subject of capitalists and capitalism: Seattle is getting its own Monopoly game. Seattle will be the second Washington city to get a Monopoly game. The first city to earn that distinction was, appropriately, Bellevue. You can weigh in on what should be included on the Seattle gameboard here . Considering our love of the free market, perhaps Seattle’s only newspaper, The Stranger , should get a spot?

Driver charged in fatal LA bus crash: The driver who was high, drove the wrong way down a busy street, ran a red light, and plowed into a Los Angeles city bus, killing two bus riders , has been charged with second-degree murder. While covering the crash, an NBC4 Los Angeles news helicopter crashed, killing a reporter, the pilot, and a pedestrian on the street.

A crazy Texas race: A seat on the overlooked, influential Texas Railroad Commission—the three-member board that regulates the oil and gas industry—is coming down to Joe Rosenthal, a Democrat who has worked in and around the subject matter for decades, and Bo French, a virulently racist Christian Nationalist. Rosenthal thought he’d be facing the seat’s incumbent, a regular Republican too cozy with oil and gas to do the job well. Nope. French, an investor and former chair of the Tarrant County GOP, openly advocates for ethnic cleansing. He’s wild enough that members of his racist party have spoken out against his racism (for example, posting a picture of South Asian University of Texas graduates and writing “the problem is now obviously far worse than anyone imagined.”) And yet, French may win. Mother Jones has more here .

What if Katie Wilson gave us the same green bus shelters those lucky ducks in New York are getting. Green roofs on their bus shelters! We should do the same. Though, we’d have to actually have functional bus shelters and adequate late-night service first. (On the subject of bus shelters, they don’t count as bus stops . articles.title: This Israeli election could be the country’s last – this week I saw that for myself | Jonathan Freedland
articles.author: Jonathan Freedland
paras: Spend time on the ground and you see how high the stakes are for next month’s contest – for Israelis and Palestinians alike

Candidates always say it, but this time it’s true. When Israel goes to the polls on 27 October , it really will be the most important election in the country’s history – and not just for Israelis. I saw that for myself this last week, in a visit that served as a sharp reminder of both what is at stake – and the role of those watching from afar.

More than one voter I spoke to voiced the fear that, if the coalition headed by Benjamin Netanyahu is returned to power next month, 27 October will not merely be Israel’s most important election: it will be its last. They were not referring to the absence of democracy in the occupied territory of the West Bank – which we’ll come to – but rather to Israel’s internationally recognised, pre-1967 borders: what you might call Israel-proper. There, the last four years have seen a sustained assault on the machinery of liberal democracy by the most rightwing government since Israel’s establishment in 1948 – a committed, focused attempt to remove the checks and restraints on its own power, installing instead a kind of elective dictatorship.
Jonathan Freedland is a Guardian columnist

articles.title: Singapore is paying people to read books – can it fix the reading crisis?
articles.author: Ella Creamer
paras: A government scheme is giving citizens cash for spending time with a good book. We ask behavioural scientists, along with The Anxious Generation author and psychologist Jonathan Haidt, whether it’ll help make the habit stick

Could the solution to the reading crisis lie in paying people to put down their phones and pick up a book? That’s what one government, at least, is resorting to: this month, Singapore launched a scheme promising actual cash to citizens as a reward for logging reading time on a government website.

It’s unlikely to make you megabucks – you have to rack up 50 reading sessions of at least 15 minutes to earn one Singapore dollar (£0.59), with only one logged session allowed per day. But behavioural scientists and psychologists told the Guardian such a scheme could still help boost a habit in precipitous decline.

articles.title: Annie Dillard brought poetry into prose, pioneering a mystical form of creative nonfiction that critics both admired and misunderstood
articles.author:
<name>Amy Cannon, Associate Professor of Writing, USC Dornsife College of Letters, Arts and Sciences</name>
      <foaf:homepage rdf:resource="https://theconversation.com/profiles/amy-cannon-1365666"/>
paras: Annie Dillard is rightly celebrated as a pioneer in creative nonfiction after her death on Sep. 15, 2026, at age 81 . But the dazzling, disorienting feel of Dillard’s work might be best understood as the often overlooked influence of poetry on her prose.

Dillard published her first full-length work of creative nonfiction, “ Pilgrim at Tinker Creek ,” when she was only 28. Winning her the 1975 Pulitzer Prize , this early book set the tone for her later work in creative nonfiction: the essay collection “ Teaching a Stone to Talk ,” and full-length works “ Holy the Firm ” and “ For the Time Being .” They all attend closely to the natural world, with a theologian’s eye and a poet’s idiom.

Dillard’s creative nonfiction about nature owes a debt to the lyrical prose of transcendentalists like Henry David Thoreau , whom Dillard cited as a major influence in her work. She was also overt about the central role that fiction played in her thinking in her book of literary criticism, “ Living by Fiction .”
But Dillard’s nonfiction, though undeniably prose, can have “ the shape and intensity of a poem ,” as her New York Times obituary puts it.
As a writer and writing professor , I think often about how blurred the boundary between poetry and prose really is. Annie Dillard’s work embodies this permeability.

Not all writing is the same. Prose typically features continuous sentences arranged in paragraphs. Poetry tends to be differentiated from prose by a deliberate organization of language that’s not determined by the page itself.

Prose poetry, the lyric essay and other hybrid forms of literature play at the intersection of genre , which usually defines these separate categories of writing. Creative nonfiction likewise aims to accurately convey reality while emphasizing literary style. The literary features of creative nonfiction are often drawn from fiction, with devices such as dialogue, scene and flashback.
But one of the distinctions of Annie Dillard’s nonfiction is how much her prose owes to poetry.

Poetry can be defined in many ways , but it tends to be characterized by honed, heightened language. Poems are often noted for their memorable images, rich sounds and foregrounding of emotion. Dillard’s nonfiction is shot through with images that arrest readers with their beauty or confront readers with their terror – as in her Harper’s essay “ The Death of a Moth ,” where the insect is drawn to a candle flame, becomes stuck in the wax and is transformed into a burning wick. In Dillard’s words:

“She burned for two hours without changing, without swaying or kneeling – only glowing within, like a building fire glimpsed through silhouetted walls, like a hollow saint, like a flame-faced virgin gone to God, while I read by her light, kindled, while Rimbaud in Paris burnt out his brain in a thousand poems, while night pooled wetly at my feet.”

It’s no accident that Dillard describes herself as reading the work of French poet Arthur Rimbaud by the light of the moth. She previously wrote that she loved how language sounds in French symbolist poetry , and Rimbaud was known to combine prose with his poetry in a way Dillard herself does.

In “ The Writing Life ,” Dillard describes the process of writing “a favorite, difficult book” – likely “Holy the Firm” – as akin to writing poetry. She notes that the writing was “so intense and accented, and the world it described was so charged with meaning,” that the idea of going further exhausted her.

To help her write, she read Conrad Aiken’s poetry aloud, describing it as “pure sound unencumbered by sense.” She would read a poetry anthology’s index of first lines because “the parallels sounded strong and suggestive.”
She also describes repeating a single line of Wallace Stevens’ poetry “for hours, like a song” while writing.
Dillard purposefully channeled poetry’s sonic density in her writing process; it comes as no surprise that the heightened register of these poems made its way into her prose.

Dillard’s virtuosic, visionary style isn’t for everyone. Writer Eudora Welty praised Dillard in her review of “Tinker Creek ,” but Welty also admitted “not (knowing) what she’s talking about” at times and that her writing “leaves something to be desired.” That something was what Welty called “straight narrative,” the clarity of “point, direction, and shape” more often demanded of prose than poetry.

The solitude of the narrator in Dillard’s nonfiction and her apparent disengagement with society also was a source of criticism. As critic William Deresiewicz put it, “There is no economy and no society ” in “Tinker Creek.” “We don’t know how Dillard lives, or how she makes a living, or much of anything about her circumstances.” Her mix of cultural disengagement and theological concern smacked to Deresiewicz of “hypocrisy and spiritual snobbery.”

In the contained world of lyric poetry, especially nature poetry, this hermetic perspective would be less of a fault. Her mystical encounters with the divine through the natural world are reminiscent of poets like Gerard Manley Hopkins , Wendell Berry and Mary Oliver . The narrow lens of her attention can be viewed as a poetic feature played out at length over her nonfiction essays and books.

Like an expressionist painting , poetry draws attention to how something is being depicted, not just what is being portrayed. Prose can do this, too – creative nonfiction, especially, and Annie Dillard’s writing most of all.
