articles.title: At-home drug disposal products can play an important role in keeping rural Coloradans safe
articles.author:
<name>Sunny Linnebur, Professor of Geriatric Pharmacy, University of Colorado Anschutz</name>
      <foaf:homepage rdf:resource="https://theconversation.com/profiles/sunny-linnebur-2712068"/>
paras: Some Coloradans have a drug problem: old prescription medications clogging their medicine cabinets.

Disposing of unused prescription and over-the-counter drugs is important to protect children and teens from accidental or unintentional exposure. Eliminating medications properly is also important to prevent contamination of vegetation, aquatic life and water supplies.

The Food and Drug Administration recommends disposing of drugs by dropping them off at a take-back location or by mailing them using a prepaid envelope that is delivered to a facility where the drugs are incinerated. These envelopes are available at some pharmacies and online.

In Colorado, the state-funded Medication and Sharps Takeback program has collected over 400,000 pounds – roughly 181 metric tons – of drugs since its inception in 2016. Medications can be dropped off at over 300 state-funded or independent drop-off sites across the state.

National take-back events in April and October each year are another way to properly dispose of medications. The drugs collected are incinerated and become irretrievable, helping keep the public and environment safe .

I am a professor of pharmacy with a focus on older adults and medication safety . For over a decade, I have co-chaired the Safe Disposal work group for the Colorado Consortium for Prescription Drug Abuse Prevention .

Although these national and statewide programs make an important difference, there are still gaps – especially for Coloradans who live in rural communities. Let’s look at the different options these consumers have:
The FDA recommends flushing some medications down the toilet.

This should be a last resort reserved for dangerous medications, like fentanyl patches, that need to be disposed of quickly to prevent them from accidentally coming into contact with other humans or pets.
Putting medications down a sink or toilet deposits them directly into wastewater, where they will likely not be filtered out .
Depositing medications into household trash also carries risks, like making them accessible to animals and other people. Drugs can leach into soil and ground water groundwater at the landfill.
At-home disposal products are a useful alternative, especially in rural areas where drug take-back programs are not readily accessible.

These products dissolve and degrade, bind up or neutralize medications so they can safely be thrown away. Disposal products come in a variety of different sizes and offer different features, so I worked with staff at University of Colorado Anschutz to test some of the popular brands to see how they worked.
The Pill Terminator is a one-time use bottle filled with a powder that turns into a gelatinous substance once medications and water are added. All pills need to be added at the same time.
We attempted adding around 30 pills to the bottle – much less than the stated 300 medium-sized pills that it could accommodate.

We observed several shortcomings. When warm water was used and the bottle was shaken, the powder was fully converted to gelatin and dissolved most of the pills. But there were still some intact pills remaining. When cold water was used, even extensive shaking did not completely dissolve the powder at the bottom of the container. Intact capsules also remained trapped within the gelatin, meaning some medications could still be identified and potentially retrieved.
The Deterra Drug Deactivation System is a biodegradable pouch that uses activated charcoal to adsorb medications after warm water is added.
According to the manufacturer, the system is designed to deactivate organic medications including opioids, most illicit drugs and vape fluid in different forms like pills, liquid and patches.

Deterra cannot adsorb biologic drugs, such as vaccines and injectable immunotherapies, nor can it adsorb inorganic medications, like iron, calcium, aluminum, magnesium and lithium. Leaf marijuana is also excluded.

Although the product label says to “gently shake,” we needed to shake the Deterra pouch more vigorously to effectively break down the medication. Most medications began to degrade relatively quickly, and the majority of pills were broken down by the water-charcoal mixture. Like with the Pill Terminator, the instruction to use warm water significantly improved the product’s performance compared with cold water.

Despite these favorable results, we observed some limitations: After several hours, extended-release capsule beads were still visible within the charcoal water, standard capsules were only partially degraded, and some sustained-release tablets remained intact.

The manufacturer states that the average time to deactivate 89% of the medication is eight hours; two days for 96%; and two weeks for 99%-100%. The pouch is not designed to be reopened, so after our initial testing, we were unable to verify these claims.

The NarcX+ disposal system is a biodegradable liquid in a plastic bottle , which can be opened and used multiple times until the bottle is full. It is the only product marketed for at-home disposal of illicit and controlled substances such as fentanyl, cocaine, heroin and cannabis, in addition to prescription and over-the-counter medications.

Initial observations after several minutes showed limited medication breakdown. However, substantial changes occurred with longer exposure. The manufacturer of NarcX+ states that medications become irretrievable in less than two hours, and consuming any of the NarcX+ liquid will cause vomiting.

We filled the NarcX+ bottle almost three-quarters full, and after four hours almost all of the pills were dissolved. At five days, the liquid in the bottle looked virtually the same, with several white sustained-release tablets still floating at the top of the liquid. After a week, they finally disappeared in the dark liquid.

NarcX+ required a little more time than the other products for the tablets to be fully destroyed, but it proved to be effective at destroying a large number of pills – more than the recommended capacity. It is uniquely designed so you can reopen the bottle to continue adding medications to the fill line. NarcX+ is validated for the widest spectrum of medications.
Read more of our stories about Colorado .
For the past 13 years, Sunny Linnebur has served as the Co-Chair of the Safe Disposal Workgroup of the Colorado Consortium for Prescription Drug Abuse Prevention.

articles.title: Flood-damaged Nepal wants help from the global climate Loss and Damage Fund – but it’s waiting, along with 118 other countries
articles.author:
<name>Tarun Gopalakrishnan, Research Fellow in the Climate Policy Lab, The Fletcher School, Tufts University</name>
      <foaf:homepage rdf:resource="https://theconversation.com/profiles/tarun-gopalakrishnan-1371014"/>
paras: As it faces the enormous task of rebuilding from a deadly flood that tore through communities in the Himalayas, Nepal is seeking compensation from the international Fund for Responding to Loss and Damage – meaning from countries that are major contributors to climate change, which it blames for the disaster.
Nepal Foreign Minister Shisir Khanal said it was not merely a request for aid or charity but a demand for justice and “legal and moral liability.”

“Nepal’s greenhouse gas emissions are virtually negligible. Yet, we are paying the ultimate price for a global crisis we did not create,” Khanal told the Kathmandu Post. “The rapid melting of glaciers and these catastrophic mountain tsunamis are direct consequences of global climate change.”

Nepal’s US$20 million request is small compared to the billions of dollars in damage , but it is an important test of the Loss and Damage Fund ’s credibility. So far the fund, created during the U.N. climate conference in 2022 to respond to the impacts of climate change in developing countries, contains a fraction of the money major greenhouse gas emitters pledged to contribute, and it has paid out nothing despite requests from at least 119 nations .
It is scientifically well established that global temperatures are rising and fueling ice melt and more extreme climate and weather conditions around the world.

Increasing greenhouse gas concentrations, largely from burning fossil fuels, have pushed global temperatures so high that sea levels are rising, and shrinking glaciers and thawing permafrost are leaving mountainsides less stable . A September 2026 U.N. Environment Program report determined that it is now inevitable that the planet will warm by at least 1.5 degrees Celsius (2.7 degrees Fahrenheit) compared to temperatures before the Industrial Revolution. Communities will have to adapt to increasing hazards.

The world committed under the Paris climate agreement to try to limit warming to 1.5 C in an attempt to avoid the worst effects of climate change. But it is not on track , and many countries are paying the price.
At least 119 countries have submitted requests for money from the Loss and Damage Fund to help them respond to disasters or adapt to climate change.

About 93% of the requests as of June 2026 involved extreme events such as floods. Over three-quarters included slow-onset events, such as requests for help building the infrastructure, including sea walls, and the capabilities to adapt to sea-level rise.
Together, the requests totaled $2.8 billion – about 10 times the amount of money that had actually reached the fund.

Wealthy countries have so far pledged to give about $820 million to the Loss and Damage Fund, but they have delivered only about a third of that – $250 million to $300 million . The U.S. withdrew its support for the fund in 2025.
The fund’s board, meanwhile, has yet to disburse money for any of the requests. At the most recent board meeting in June 2026, officials considered four requests for funding, but none were approved.

The board has a responsibility to ensure that the money will be used appropriately. But one analysis of comments countries made while negotiating the creation of the fund and decisions of the fund board suggested that the slowness of both the disbursals and the setting up of the fund had been deliberate – a practical evasion of a responsibility agreed to on paper.

The board is scheduled to meet next in December 2026. Eight of the 26 board members formally requested an emergency meeting to respond to the disaster in Nepal quickly. The co-chairs of the board acknowledged the request , but how the board might respond was unclear.

Nepal is asking for about $20 million from the fund. However, the country’s finance minister, Swarnim Wagle, estimated that the country would need US$4 billion to $5 billion to rebuild from the flood damage – nearly a tenth of its national economy.

Nepal lost over 10% of its hydropower capacity when a glacier collapsed on Aug. 26, causing the landslide and flood. Mud, water and rock inundated several riverside communities near the border with China, killing more than 1,400 people and leaving thousands more missing. The flood also broke through several hydropower dams in the Bhote Koshi river basin.

In Nepal, many of the risks come from melting glaciers. The Himalayas and neighboring Hindu Kush mountains together contain one of the world’s largest volumes of ice , but studies show they have been losing that ice fast as temperatures rise, with the loss rate doubling since 2000 . When glaciers retreat, the result can create glacial lakes prone to outburst floods and unstable slopes prone to landslides like Nepal experienced .
Nepal is receiving aid directly from other countries, but it wants support from the Loss and Damage Fund in part because of what that would represent.
In many ways, the fund is symbolic, and that symbolism is important .

Vulnerable countries fought through years of international climate talks to establish a principle of climate compensation and distinguish it from charity. Even if the amount that the fund disburses to Nepal is relatively small, it would represent compensation for harm caused by climate change.

Countries are often willing to provide humanitarian assistance, but they are resistant to providing funding labeled “loss and damage,” unwilling to assume responsibility – and potentially liability – for climate change.

The decision establishing the fund is very clear that contributions are voluntary and the act of contributing should not be interpreted as an acknowledgment of liability. Climate-vulnerable countries consented to that language in the hope that it would bring in much-needed help.
If the fund acts promptly and pragmatically on that shared responsibility, global efforts to establish liability for climate change through international tribunals and courts could ease.

To be effective, the Loss and Damage Fund needs to be more agile and responsive to the needs of the most climate-vulnerable countries. During negotiations to set up the fund, one negotiator emphasized the need for resources to be accessible within 24 to 48 hours of a climate disaster .

A coalition of experienced adaptation and disaster response organizations has argued that the fund should prioritize effective existing local and national programs and low-cost and low-risk projects. These include community-based resilience and recovery with local volunteers, health centers and cash transfers to flood-affected households.

The Loss and Damage Fund could also use its symbolic and modest financial position to nudge the broader humanitarian, development and climate finance ecosystem toward what’s known as anticipatory action .
Anticipatory action involves moving resources into at-risk places before the disaster hits. It has been proven to speed up the response and recovery .
Emphasizing this approach could also lead to better forecasting, early warnings and planning that takes climate change into account to protect people in vulnerable regions around the world.

articles.title: Why the closing prayers of Judaism’s holiest holiday focus on repairing relationships with each other
articles.author:
<name>Reuven Kimelman, Professor of Classical Judaica, Brandeis University, Brandeis University</name>
      <foaf:homepage rdf:resource="https://theconversation.com/profiles/reuven-kimelman-2723789"/>
paras: Each Passover, as Jewish families start the Seder meal, a child asks, “ Why is this night different from all other nights? ”
And each Yom Kippur, as worshippers attend the last prayers of the day, they might well ask: “Why is this closing service different from all other services?”

Throughout the High Holidays , the 10-day period that begins with Rosh Hashanah and ends with Yom Kippur, Jews pray to be “inscribed” in the Book of Life – that God grant them life , livelihood, health and moral growth in the coming year.

The holidays culminate in Yom Kippur, the Day of Atonement: a day dedicated to reflection, fasting and repairing each person’s relationship with others – and through that, their relationship with God.

According to Jewish tradition, the Book of Life is sealed as Yom Kippur draws to a close , as is each person’s fate for the coming year. During the fifth and final service, one prays to be “sealed,” which on this Day of Judgment entails being forgiven. This last service is thus titled “Ne’ilah,” or “the closing,” reflecting the idea that the gates of heaven are closing . It also alludes to the gates of the ancient Temple in Jerusalem, where the holiday was once celebrated.

Ne’ilah prayers are accordingly recited at the closing of the day – just at sunset, adding nature’s drama to the closing of the day. The ambience is enhanced by keeping open the ark of the Torah , the usually closed chamber at the front of the synagogue that protects the scrolls of scripture. Many congregants remain standing, using this final chance to plead their case as the day slips by.

Yom Kippur is a day reserved for repentance, expressed through confession – and, in many ways, it is a day of repetition. The confessional prayer is recited up to 10 times over the course of five services.

It begins with the congregation asking God for forgiveness “for the sin that I have committed before You.” Yet what follows is an extended list of ethical sins, with a focus on the sins of abusive speech, such as slandering, slurring, slighting and smearing the reputations of others. A foundational concept of Judaism is that humanity is made in the image of God , meaning that in wronging others, we offend God as well.
As a scholar of Jewish liturgy , I believe this prayer points to a key theme of the entire High Holidays, and of Judaism itself: that to do right by God, people must first do right by each other .

After reciting the confessional, the Ne’ilah service adds one more prayer, not used in other services. This addendum focuses not on the specifics of confession but the dynamics of repentance : underscoring that belief that each person’s relationship with God is correlated with their relationship with other people.

Ne’ilah thus focuses on the sin of fraud, echoing a passage from the biblical Book of Jonah read in the preceding afternoon service: “Let everyone repent of their evil way by giving back the stolen goods in their hands.” To return to God, then, it is important to return what is owed to other people: emotionally, spiritually and materially.

Whereas the oft-repeated confessional focuses on offenses of the lips, such as slander, here the focus is on offenses of the hands : taking what does not belong to us, such as by exploiting the vulnerable or committing fraud.

The prayer opens with God’s outstretched, inviting hand , inducing penitents to hand over ill-gotten goods to their rightful owner. But as the addendum has it, God can’t hold out his hand in reconciliation until we have reconciled with the people we wronged.

“You give space” – literally, you give a hand – “to the sinner, but You extend Your right hand to penitents,” it begins. “You have taught us … to confess to You every one of our sins so that we cease handling unlawful goods.”

Judaism holds that God won’t forgive you for a sin if you haven’t made amends with the person you wronged . During the Days of Awe leading up to Yom Kippur, Jews are taught to ask each other for forgiveness, apologizing for the ways we wronged one another in the past year.

Rather than browbeating people into repentance, the Ne’ilah service’s strategy is to boost them up into it, playing upon the biblical idea of the grandeur of humanity. “You have distinguished humanity from the beginning, privileging it to stand before You,” the liturgy says .
Judaism sees sin as a rupture that can be healed, not an inherent condition. The liturgy’s message is this: Live up to your greatness, your divinely endowed potential, as a being made in God’s image.
For Ne’ilah, the eminence of humanity consists in the ability to repent and set things right before man and God. This is what Yom Kippur is all about.

articles.title: The ethical cases for immigration as a human right
articles.author:
<name>J. Toby Reiner, Professor of Political Science, Dickinson College</name>
      <foaf:homepage rdf:resource="https://theconversation.com/profiles/j-toby-reiner-1494313"/>
paras: U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement arrested roughly 50,000 immigrants in July and August 2026; almost 80% of those migrants did not have a criminal record. Until the end of the Biden administration, federal authorities did not expect migrants to leave the country while their visa renewal was pending . The Trump administration has changed that policy.

ICE has defended itself for the overall scale of detentions by saying that it is simply enforcing federal immigration law . However, immigrant rights advocates are skeptical about this claim and wary about the lack of oversight of ICE agents .
This scale of immigration enforcement raises fundamental philosophical questions: What ethical obligations do governments have to prospective migrants? And what claims to admission do migrants have?

As a scholar of migration ethics , I have studied the arguments philosophers make about migration. Many philosophers claim that immigration should be understood as a human right. From their perspective, governments have an important responsibility to tread carefully when denying entry to migrants and especially when deporting them.
To consider the moral foundations of criticisms of ICE, it is useful to first examine the arguments in favor of freedom of movement.

Several philosophers have argued for freedom of movement, often on the grounds that migration should be understood as a human right . For example, the philosopher Kieran Oberman argues that people have a basic interest in being able to move to any country in which they have core attachments, such as a job or close family members. This argument follows the claim, developed by philosophers such as John Stuart Mill and John Rawls, that individuals should be free to pursue their own life plans . They hold that this pursuit is essential to achieving self-realization.

The argument for freedom of movement often involves a comparison to movement within a nation-state. At least in liberal democracies, citizens are entitled to move anywhere they wish within state borders. Political philosopher Joseph Carens uses this claim when he argues that freedom of international movement is justified as an extension of internal freedom of movement .

Citizens may move where they wish within state borders because this protects freedom. This includes both the freedom to pursue important personal projects and goals, and to pursue joint projects such as business endeavors .

The freedom-based argument for migration maintains that the same considerations that apply within a country also do so internationally . For example, immigration restrictions can prevent people from marrying their preferred partner or from pursuing the job of their dreams.
If we value freedom, we have a reason to allow people to work, study and live wherever they wish because doing so may be integral to a fulfilling life.

If migration were a human right, then any state-imposed restriction on movement across borders would constitute an unjust violation of rights. According to this perspective, then, states do not have the right to control immigration .
Underlying this view is a conception of human rights in which rights take precedence over other values , such as social welfare, because they protect vital human interests.

Against this view, other philosophers hold that societies rely for their cohesion on some degree of cultural commonality . In this view – echoed by many political critics of mass migration – unless political communities have shared values, they will be unstable .

A related argument made by philosophers such as Sarah Song and Michael Walzer is that control over migration is integral to self-determination. Without it, states cannot be sovereign entities that decide for themselves what shape their society should take. They cannot produce “communities of character”: social groups that share a way of life that they wish to pass on to their descendants .

But some philosophers argue national sovereignty cannot override people’s equality of opportunity – a key goal of liberal democracies. Migration could serve a way to expand opportunities across borders.

In this view, restrictions on migration render citizenship a form of feudal privilege in an unequal world; they deny people from poorer countries the chance to access opportunities and resources in wealthier economies .

This argument holds, then, that restrictions on migration fix a global hierarchy in place, reduce social mobility and give people unearned advantages based on where they happened to be born. Moreover, they do this using all the tools of violence at the state’s disposal.
As with the freedom argument, this claim hopes to appeal to both the left and the right, for equality of opportunity is a bipartisan political value.

In addition, scholars such as the political geographer Reece Jones argue that migration restrictions reinforce global racial inequalities . As Jones notes, the migrants who are denied admission to the U.S., and to Western European countries, are predominantly from countries in the Global South that are majority nonwhite.

Advocates of the equality argument often hold that migration will not merely promote equality of opportunity but also reduce economic inequality. This is because opportunities to access social welfare, healthcare and other important social goods are often greater in wealthier economies.

For example, the philosopher Darrel Moellendorf argues that children should have the same opportunity to become a banker wherever in the world they are born . Moellendorf holds that, if there were global equality of opportunity, a child born in Mozambique would have the same chance of becoming an investment banker as would one born in Switzerland. Migration is thus a crucial means of enabling people born in the Global South to access lucrative jobs .

There are many objections to this proposal . For example, Song points out that different societies regard different opportunities as important. It therefore might not be possible to come up with a global list of opportunities that should be equal .

Yet the equality of opportunity argument gets to the core of the dispute about migration. Liberal democracies understand themselves to be committed to meritocracy. This requires that individuals rise and fall based on their own talents.
As migration restrictions deny people opportunities based on where they were born, they may be in tension with fundamental democratic principles.

articles.title: Pete Hegseth is rebuilding the Army’s ‘brass ceiling’
articles.author:
<name>Jeremiah Favara, Associate Professor of Communication Studies, Gonzaga University</name>
      <foaf:homepage rdf:resource="https://theconversation.com/profiles/jeremiah-favara-1427916"/>
paras: Dan Driscoll resigned as secretary of the Army on Aug. 31, 2026. His departure leaves the Army without a Senate-confirmed civilian leader six months into the war with Iran, its busiest period since the wars in Iraq and Afghanistan.

Driscoll’s resignation was reportedly motivated, at least in part, by his frustration with Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth . Earlier in August, Hegseth had blocked the promotions of four Army officers.

Since his appointment in January 2025, Hegseth has fired or blocked the promotions of more than 80 admirals and generals . Often, Hegseth has referenced “woke” diversity efforts in his reasoning. One officer who was blocked had written a paper while in graduate school about the impact of political polarization on recruiting . Another officer had his name pulled from the promotion list after officials incorrectly believed that he had allowed a mentorship group for female paratroopers to exist in his unit.
More than half of the officers removed have been women or Black in an officer corps that is 79% male and 74% white .

Hegseth’s blocking of promotions and apparent targeting of women and Black people appear to violate military rules meant to protect against the politicization of the military’s officer corps and have undermined faith in the military’s promotion system , which is supposed to be merit-based.

I’ve spent years studying the U.S. military and have written a book on diversity and military recruiting . In my assessment, Hegseth is building a military that fits a narrow ideological view at the cost of its service members’ safety and well-being.
The Army exceeded its recruiting goal of 60,500 new enlistees in fiscal year 2025 and has already hit its targets for the 2026 fiscal year.

In fact, 2026 marks the third straight year that every active duty military service has met its recruiting goals . That the Army and other branches have been able to do this – despite the fact that they rely on women and people of color – would, at first glance, seem to indicate that the politicization of the military has not hurt recruiting.

Hegseth has attributed the success to “the belief (recruits) have in civilian leadership and military leadership.” According to a Pentagon spokesperson , “Americans everywhere are prouder than ever to serve.”
What Hegseth and others fail to acknowledge, however, is that recruitment is driven not by ideology but by market factors and need.

Since the end of the draft in 1973, according to my research, the success of military recruiting has largely hinged on young people’s perceptions of their chances for upward mobility. Many young people join the military because they are in need of the opportunities military service provides. This past year’s recruitment numbers are likely more a result of young Americans seeking steady pay, job training and educational benefits than agreement with Hegseth’s vision of the military.

Market research studies conducted in the past year have found that making money, paying for education, travel, work experience and medical benefits are the top motivators guiding young people toward military service. Recruits are guided by what military sociologist Charles C. Moskos called occupational appeals that frame enlisting as a smart economic decision rather than by patriotism or nationalism. These kinds of appeals have historically been successful in attracting the diverse recruits – women and people of color – who have been critical to the military’s ability to meet its personnel needs .

Recruiting data shows that Hegseth and other members of the Trump administration have little control over the composition of the enlisted ranks. However, Hegseth’s anti-woke campaign is changing what the military is like for those who serve.
Historically, women, Black service members and service members of color have faced discrimination and violence within the ranks .

Recent firings and blocked promotions have further shaped a military leadership that has historically been almost exclusively white and male. All five service chiefs and 9 in 10 combatant commanders are white men . This year the lowest percentage of women in 25 years have been nominated to the rank of general and admiral.

This targeting of women and people of color has solidified the “brass ceiling” – a term used to describe the limited opportunities for promotion for women and Black service members – and is creating a military leadership that doesn’t reflect the service members they command or the nation they represent. The overwhelmingly white and male leadership commands an enlisted force in which 34% identify with a racial minority group and 17% are women .

By purging military leadership of women, Black service members and those who have supported opportunities for service members other than white men, Hegseth is creating a culture ripe for racial, sexual and gender discrimination and harassment.

Hegseth has also sought to restore tributes to Confederate soldiers and has attacked military diversity. These actions further erase and invalidate the contributions of women, Black service members and other service members of color.
The military’s need for more equitable representation was born of the demands and costs of combat.
During the Vietnam War, disproportionate numbers of Black and Latino service members served in combat and were killed while under the command of a largely white officer corps.

The Defense Race Relations Institute – now known as the Defense Equal Opportunity Management Institute – was formed in 1971 to provide race relations education to every member of the armed forces to quell rampant racial unrest, including racial violence and fragging incidents. Fragging incidents – the killing of a fellow service member, often using fragmentation grenades – were rampant in Vietnam.

Army Reserve Officers’ Training Corps programs were instituted at historically Black colleges and universities to increase the numbers of Black officers. The Department of Defense pushed for increased ROTC programs at HBCUs during the Vietnam war as a way to increase the size of the officer corps.

While HBCUs provided large numbers of Black officers during Vietnam , the success of diversifying the officer corps has been limited. Scholars have attributed this limited success, despite consistent efforts to recruit Black Americans, to educational inequalities and the conservative culture of the officer corps.
These efforts were based on the military adopting the idea that an efficient and lethal military should look like the nation it serves and that its leaders should look like the soldiers they command.

Hegseth’s purging of the officer ranks means the Americans who serve in the military won’t see themselves reflected in leadership or see a path to the top ranks. But they will continue to bear the costs of war: About half of the 18 service members killed in the Iran war between February and August were women and people of color.

articles.title: Seattle’s KEXP eyes a second physical home — in San Francisco’s historic Haight-Ashbury
articles.author: Kurt Schlosser
paras: Seattle independent radio station KEXP is exploring the possibility of building out a second physical home — far from its beloved base at Seattle Center — in San Francisco.

Three years after expanding its broadcast footprint to the Bay Area with the acquisition of 92.7 KREV FM, the non-profit music institution has set its sights on the city’s historic Haight-Ashbury neighborhood for a potential site.

Under a proposed partnership announced Thursday by KEXP and city preservation group SF Heritage , the station would team up with local nonprofit Blue Bear School of Music to convert the historic Doolan-Larson House and Storefronts at the corner of Haight and Ashbury streets into a multifaceted music and cultural center.

The early-stage plan for the landmark property envisions radio broadcast facilities, a roof venue for live performances and community events, space for group and individual music lessons, and a public “third space” intended for year-round daily gathering.

The proposed hub adds another twist to the long-standing cross-pollination between the two tech capitals. While Silicon Valley giants have routinely set up major engineering outposts in Seattle, and founders and workers migrate between the regions, KEXP’s expansion represents a rare cultural export heading in the opposite direction.
San Francisco Mayor Daniel Lurie cheered the proposal as a win for both the neighborhood and the city’s broader economic recovery.

“Art and music have been part of what makes San Francisco special for generations,” Lurie said in a statement. “Innovative partnerships like this one help us reimagine what’s possible and find new ways to activate our neighborhoods. Our artists and cultural spaces make our city stronger, and this new home for music and culture at Haight and Ashbury will inspire generations to come.”

Located at the epicenter of the 1960s counterculture movement, the Colonial Revival-style Doolan-Larson House was originally constructed in 1903 and raised after the 1906 San Francisco earthquake to add ground-floor storefronts.

The property — designated San Francisco Landmark No. 253 and listed on the National Register of Historic Places — housed groundbreaking hippie-era boutiques during the Summer of Love. It was gifted to SF Heritage in 2017 by its long-time owner, the late Norman Larson, specifically to ensure the landmark would be preserved and activated for public and cultural use.

Founded in 1972 as KCMU — a small, student-run station at the University of Washington — KEXP has spent over five decades building a global reputation for human-curated music discovery, famously becoming one of the first stations to champion the “Seattle sound” in the late 1980s.

The station’s Bay Area presence officially materialized in late 2023 when KEXP placed the winning $3.75 million bid at a bankruptcy auction to acquire commercial frequency 92.7 KREV FM (now KEXC). Funded by a portion of a $10 million bequest left by a anonymous long-time donor, the station began retransmitting its broadcast signal to Northern California in March 2024 as part of a strategy to ground its growing digital and streaming audience in key cultural markets.

In Seattle, KEXP’s physical hub at Seattle Center — itself a civic landmark — features a public Gathering Space that combines a coffee shop, record store, and live performance venue alongside its open-view DJ booth.

Translating a high-touch, human-centered physical experience into new markets is a core priority for the station: KEXP recently hired its first chief product and technology officer, former SiriusXM and Nordstrom executive Jyoti Shukla, to build digital products and physical spaces that intentionally prioritize human music curation over AI algorithms.

In a post on LinkedIn , KEXP CEO Ethan Raup said the response to the station’s arrival in the Bay Area “has been nothing short of remarkable” and that it gave KEXP “the confidence to start planning for our next big step.”

In its post on Thursday, KEXP stressed the plans are “not a done deal yet.” Over the coming months, SF Heritage, KEXP, and Blue Bear School of Music will focus on gathering community feedback, finalizing an adaptive reuse plan, and determining construction feasibility and project financing.
KEXP and Blue Bear representatives will make their first public outreach push at the Haight Ashbury Street Fair on Sunday to share more about the proposed project.

articles.title: Seattle's Speed Camera Program Enters New Frontier
articles.author: Ryan Packer
paras: Seattle is set to see four new automatic speed cameras in 2027, but it's not the number of cameras that will make the move notable. The cameras will be the city's first full-time speed cameras, after decades of keeping automatic speed cameras confined to time-limited school zones.
The Urbanist's Fall Member Drive is in full swing! Support our work, read ad-free, and help us hit our goal for the member drive!

Drivers will encounter the cameras along E Marginal Way S, and Sand Point Way NE, and two different segments of Rainier Avenue S – locations where driver speeds are consistently much higher than posted speed limits. Exact cross-streets where the cameras will be installed are still being determined, according to an announcement from the Seattle Department of Transportation (SDOT).

SDOT also maintains a constellation of red light cameras, along with less common cameras tasked with enforcing bus-only lanes and intersection blocking. The authority to put up a 24/7 camera away from a school zone comes from a 2024 overhaul to state law governing camera use that was codified into city code last year.

While the issue of the Seattle Police Department's CCTV camera network has been an incredible contentious one during Mayor Katie Wilson's first months in office, a clearer political consensus has emerged around automatic traffic cameras. Unlike CCTV cameras, significant guardrails govern the use of traffic cameras by state law, including the inability for traffic camera footage to be turned over to officers investigating other crimes.

Wilson's executive order accelerating work on traffic safety projects, released on August 21, included a commitment to add 10 cameras to the city's arsenal by early 2029, with these four cameras representing a down payment on that promise.

"Everyone needs to get around safely, and we are committed to our goal of ending deadly crashes and serious injuries in Seattle. As we work to accelerate traffic safety projects throughout the city, we’re moving forward with new 24/7 speed safety cameras in four locations with a history of excessive speeding and deadly crashes," the department wrote in a blog post last week touting the move.

Two of the new cameras – along E Marginal Way and Sand Point Way – will be located along streets that have a posted speed limit that is higher than the city's default arterial limit of 25 mph. But Seattle's 2025 annual traffic report shows that drivers are still regularly exceeding the speed limit there. For example, despite a 30 mph limit along Sand Point Way, the 85th percentile speed – the speed at or below which 85% of drivers travel – was somewhere between 35 to 40 mph.

"Our data shows that 15% of people driving in all four of these locations were traveling 10+ mph over the speed limit," the blog post continued. "Our goal was to boost safety where it’s most needed, while trying to avoid over-concentration of cameras in historically disadvantaged neighborhoods."

Normalized, excessive speeding increases the risk of crash severity significantly, especially for people traveling around the city by walking, biking, or rolling. According to the Insurance Institute for Highway Safety , a pedestrian struck at 20 mph has an 18% chance of sustaining a serious injury, but at 35 mph, the risk of serious injury climbs to 67%. Those risks are intensified thanks to the fondness for larger vehicle types in the U.S. compared to elsewhere in the world.

The issue of equitable camera placement has been front-and-center in the conversation around traffic camera expansion in Seattle over recent years. When SDOT was deciding how to double the school zone camera program in 2023, the department consciously selected school locations in more affluent areas in order to balance out camera locations that had been placed in neighborhoods with higher minority populations.

Several of the streets poised for 24/7 speed camera installation are also set to see physical upgrades that have the potential to reduce driver speeds through improved design. In Rainier Beach, SDOT is advancing plans to revamp Rainier Avenue between S Henderson Street and Ithaca Place S, as well as make changes to Seward Park Avenue S between Henderson and Rainier – including the interim installation of a new marked crossing and signal at Rainier Avenue S and 54th Avenue S by the end of the year.

On north Rainier Avenue, an even more substantive street rebuild remains in early stages, in an area where traffic safety advocates have been pushing for changes for years . That repaving project, being paired with a repave of S Henderson in Rainier Beach with a combined budget of more than $100 million dollars, is not set to be fully wrapped up until 2032.

Other cities around the region are also taking advantage of state's new camera authority, going even further than Seattle. Earlier this summer, Edmonds City Council voted to convert existing time-limited cameras at four different schools to 24/7 operation, citing the need to improve safety conditions around schools outside of the 90 minutes surrounding bell times on school days. Over a two-week period this summer, nearly 20,000 citations would have been issued to drivers traveling at least seven miles per hour over the normal speed limit, had the camera hours been expanded already.

Across Lake Washington in Bellevue, four new sets of 24/7 speed cameras near hospitals, parks, and school walk zones were installed in August, with another three locations eyed for implementation by the end of the year. Those new cameras garnered headlines when they were vandalized less than a week after installation , but that only represented a small setback for Bellevue's traffic camera program.

articles.title: Kelabe Tewolde Is the Real Deal
articles.author: Harry Cheadle
paras: On an August evening in Beacon Hill, in the back patio of the restaurant familyfriend, Kelabe Tewolde and his crew hovered around a laptop, waiting for the first primary election results to come in. As a first-time candidate, Tewolde hoped to get at least 40 percent of the vote. That would prove the progressive challenger had a serious shot at unseating Rep. Sharon Tomiko Santos, who has represented the 37th District since 1999.

The primary election was a mixed bag for Seattle progressives, particularly those hoping to unseat incumbents. Hannah Sabio-Howell’s relatively high-profile campaign against State Senate Majority Leader Jamie Pedersen hit a snag: she won just 24 percent of the vote. In Northeast Seattle’s 46th District, State Representative Gerry Pollet won over half the vote, beating out a pair of progressives. But Tewolde had a good night.

When the results came in, Tewolde’s supporters cheered. Tewolde exceeded expectations , winning 46 percent of the initial vote tally. As more ballots trickled in over the coming days, that number climbed to 51 percent, leaving Santos solidly in second.

Going into the general election, the contest for Santos’s State House seat is now one of the most hotly contested races in King County. It pits a young, progressive renter against an older homeowner and member of the local political establishment. Tewolde besting Santos was a longshot before the primary, but now he could be this year’s surprise political success story.

The 37th is an oblong district that stretches from Madrona and the Chinatown-International District in the north down the east side of I-5 to Skyway and Bryn Mawr in the south. It’s one of the most diverse areas in the entire country, home to immigrant communities from all over Asia and Africa. It’s where Tewolde’s single mother, a refugee from Eritrea, found herself in 1994.

She struggled to afford housing, moving her family of two frequently, sometimes staying with extended family in South Seattle, sometimes living in public housing, or moving constantly to different rentals in North Seattle. There were years when they didn’t have a car and neighbors brought Tewolde to and from school. At his primary election party Tewolde said he and his mother were supported by “the dopest village ever,” a network of “aunties, uncles, and older cousins” who could help out.
When Tewolde was a child his grandmother, who essentially raised him until he was nine, died of lymphoma, leaving the family buried in medical debt. His mother had to declare bankruptcy.
His mother hid how desperate her economic circumstances were. “She made it seem like we were middle-class,” Tewolde says, “but we were pretty low on the totem pole.”

The summer after fifth grade, Tewolde got into Rainier Scholars , a nonprofit that helps underserved youth prepare for college. With assistance from that program and some prodding from his mother, he went to University Prep on a scholarship beginning in the seventh grade. That put him on a path to studying political science at Colgate, a private university in Upstate New York. He interned with US Senator Patty Murray, imagining a career as a political staffer. Instead, he wound up back at Rainier Scholars as an academic counselor in 2018, helping the kids who were in the same position he was in a decade earlier.

When the COVID-19 pandemic shut down the world, Tewolde helped organize an effort by local restaurants like Musang and Lil Woody’s to get meals to food-insecure people. It was a “community effort,” he says and his role was “behind the scenes,” which suited him. He’s not someone who seeks the spotlight.

For a political candidate, Tewolde seems low-key; he’s not shy or awkward, but he doesn’t have the polished, glad-handing charisma that longtime politicians acquire. He dislikes candidates who make their campaigns all about them, the ones who say, “Get behind me.”

He didn’t think of himself as candidate material until this past year, when he met people at the progressive Working Families Party who encouraged him to consider running for office. With his strong ties to the community and educator background, he could help the progressive cause in Olympia. There was even an open spot in the 37th; Rebecca Saldaña left her State Senate position to run for King County Council, and kickstarted a game of political musical chairs. With Rep. Chipalo Street from the 37th running for Saldaña’s seat, Tewolde considered running for Street’s seat, but progressive Jaelynn Scott was already vying for it. He didn’t want to oppose Scott—“I’d rather vote for her,” he says. (Scott easily won her primary and is on track to become Washington’s first trans legislator.) Instead, he eyed a harder target: Santos, who had represented the district since Tewolde was four years old.

Sabio-Howell helped convince Tewolde to run against Santos just as she was running against Pedersen. She called him and, as she told The Stranger , said, “‘it’s time to get establishment leadership in fighting shape or out of the way.’” A progressive challenge would be beneficial regardless of who won, she reasoned. If the longtime incumbents prevailed, they might have to commit to progressive ideas including “protections for renters” and “taxes on corporations,” she says. “It’s through these challenges that we move the issues forward.” Tewolde agreed. The race was on.

Tewolde says that he’s trying to run a “respectful” campaign. He told the Hacks and Wonks podcast this summer that Santos “has a long legacy of doing right by the district, but… more recently has started to stray away from the progressive values of the 37th.” One of his major points of contention with her is that she was the only Seattle-area politician to vote against a rent stabilization bill last year.

That vote, Santos says, was motivated by her conviction that the bill was “a blunt approach to a problem that needed a fine-edged scalpel.” She was concerned that smaller landlords struggling from rising costs would be hurt by a cap on rent increases, Santos told The Stranger . Tewolde thinks “it’s wild” for a 27-year incumbent “to not be in favor of some sort of stabilization” when renters are now a majority in the district. “I’ve moved four times in the last six years,” he says, once because “the rent was too dang high.” He worries that when families are forced to move because they can’t afford housing—like his mother had to—it disrupts the lives of their children.
“When a kid moves, it throws everything off in their education journey,” he says.

Beyond the specific policy disputes with Santos, Tewolde is offering voters a fresh face. Democrats around the country are unhappy with party leadership and incumbents, and some of that dissatisfaction may be trickling down to South Seattle. Tewolde says that even when he knocks on doors near Seward Park—one of the district’s wealthiest neighborhoods—he’s gotten positive responses. “I was surprised that there were people that were pretty friendly and also interested in change,” he says, with some people saying, “‘Yeah, we need new leadership.’”

King County Executive Girmay Zahilay, Tewolde’s most prominent endorser, compared himself to Tewolde. Both men are sons of East African refugees and both experienced housing insecurity growing up in South Seattle. Zahilay won election to the King County Council in 2019 by defeating longtime incumbent, Larry Gossett. Tewolde could do the same if voters believe he embodies a new vision for the district.

“Kelabe is an educator and housing advocate who has spent his career investing in the community he’s from,” Zahilay said in a statement to The Stranger. “The 37th has always been special, and it’s ready for the next step.”

Sabio-Howell thinks that if Tewolde pushed Santos to make some progressive policy commitments, that would count as a win. But Tewolde isn’t interested in moral victories. “The time to push her toward progressive policy has passed,” he says of Santos. “I’m running to win so this district has a representative who shows up for the 37th.” He just might be able to.

For the next two months, Tewolde is living the life of a small-time candidate. He’s raised just over $82,600. He hasn’t hired a campaign manager, knocking on doors and dialing donors himself when he’s not working at Rainier Scholars.

Santos, who hasn’t faced many serious challengers in her political career, acknowledged to the Washington State Standard that she’s working harder than she has before. She’s outraised Tewolde, boasting a war chest of $140,000 and she’s endorsed by more politicians. But Tewolde is backed by Chris Reykdal, the state Superintendent of Public Instruction, and in a recent endorsement from the Seattle Times editorial board, the board called out Santos, the chair of the House Education committee, for her lack of vision on education.

Since the primary, more people are picking up Tewolde’s calls. He’s not just a candidate—he’s someone who can win. It’s a real race. “With those results, a lot of people are taking it more seriously,” he says.
The post Kelabe Tewolde Is the Real Deal appeared first on The Stranger .

articles.title: Girls Own the Void and Art Owns Downtown
articles.author: Amanda Manitach
paras: The second half of September means Art + Culture Week is upon us. Recall how I previously mentioned September is Art World Prom in NYC? This week feels like a (much-needed) attempt to recalibrate the Seattle art calendar to match some of that energy. Now in its third year, the annual Art + Culture Week festival is designed to stack as many events as possible at as many galleries and venues as possible within the space of nine days. It’s a great way to get to know new spaces or get to know old ones better. Find the complete calendar of events here .

The keynote event is WALKDONTRUN , now in its second year, which turns downtown into an art-filled corridor. It’s gonna be gorgeous out, so unless you’re going to a wedding or a funeral, you better soak it up. Here are details about that plus some other things I recommend you catch in the coming weeks.

September 17 unpoetry at Frye Art Museum Our Genius shortlister Eric M. Acosta brings ekphrasis to life with the latest installation of unpoetry at the Frye . This one is inspired by the current exhibit I hear the hollow boom of time , with responsive works by dance artist Noelle Chun; composer, intermedia artist, poet, and archivist María Dolores A. Matienzo; and multi-instrumentalist Tom Scully, who is currently the guitarist for improvised noise duo CSTMR and “gunk-pop” band Black Ends. Project NW: David Hytone at Tacoma Art Museum For the past decade, David Hytone has been building a style and process that produces visual stunners—uncanny mixed-media quasi-landscapes on canvas that are populated with hypothetical dream architecture and objects not from the “real” world. His Project NW installation at Tacoma Art Museum leans even harder into nostalgia-tinged dream imagery and gently absurd symbolism (sinking toy ships and carnival roller coasters). He’s also utilized the space to introduce some massive pieces that tip traditional painting into the realm of installation.

September 17-19 The Goldberg Variations at On the Boards The word “unhinged” is the primary adjective used to describe Clayton Lee’s The Goldberg Variations , opening this week at On the Boards . What’s actually going to unfold onstage tonight is a surprise—each performance is different (you can read a review of the recent iteration at Portland’s Time-Based Art Festival here ), but I daresay we’ll be enraptured as Lee uses Bach and wrestling as a vehicle for teasing out fantasies delving into themes of “power dynamics, sexual desire, and vulnerability that entangles queer sexuality with classical music and professional wrestling.”

September 19 WALKDONTRUN The long-awaited WALKDONTRUN features more than 200 artists spread across 20 blocks of downtown Seattle. Find the full list here . This year, the route is reversed from last year’s, kicking off in Westlake Park at 11 a.m. and ending at Occidental Square. Here are my notes from print: Last year’s wayfinding was a little tricky. If that’s the case again, my advice is to study the route beforehand and plot a path so you don’t miss artists like Dez’Mon Omega Fair , one of my favorite performance artists in town; Charmi Shah , who is hiding collectable, baseball-card-size collages along the route for participants to find and keep; and Jesse Higman , whose interactive paint-pouring technique, performed around a massive tilting table , is an unforgettable experience. Or just wander blindly and let the art happen to you, because the magic of this event is that you get to experience the city in a completely new way.

Cut the Red Tape at Slip Gallery Seattle was shaped by redlining, a discriminatory housing practice that involved denying mortgages, insurance, or other financial services to Black, Asian American, and other communities of color in certain neighborhoods, resulting in wealth disparities and racial segregation. At Slip Gallery , Rodney King’s Cut the Red Tape addresses this city’s history of redlining and on Saturday the gallery hosts a panel discussion (noon–2 pm) featuring King and guest artists Myron Curry, TR Miles, Vincent Keele, and Jonarra Swanson to discuss gentrification, redlining, and how artists can shape what society remembers.

Social Contract at Actualize AiR Tommy Gregory and Rachael Comer have curated the fall exhibition at Actualize AiR , which features 17 artists from across the continental US, including The Stranger’ s very own Charles Mudede, whose video, Twilight of the Goodtimes , loops across a TV screen haunted by the fallout of late capitalism’s repeated calamities. I’m here for it. An opening reception is scheduled during WALKDONTRUN (4–8 pm) with an artist talk at 5.

September 20 Build Your Own Black Hole at Steve Gilbert Studio Do astrophysics the hedgewitch way with Meghan Thréinfhir ’s Build Your Own Black Hole workshop, from 3–6 pm at Steve Gilbert Studio . Thréinfhir will take you through her solo exhibition, Spacetime Gothic, which features her original black hole in a jar—an inky, liquidy ball of ferrofluid that dances with magnets and has the impeccable title Girls Own The Void (Land Art For Bog Witches) . All materials provided but the vessel—just bring a small jar, baby-food size recommended.

September 23 William Kentridge Anything Is Possible at Greg Kucera Gallery It’s movie night in the gallery. They’re screening the feature documentary William Kentridge Anything Is Possible along with short films by the artist (6–7:30 pm). The doc provides a BTS glimpse inside Kentridge’s studio practice and mind. The selection of shorts, featuring hand-drawn charcoal animations, explores his themes of memory, time, and all kinds of politics-ridden history.

September 24 Day-to-Day: A Life in Sticky Notes at Henry Art Gallery Artist Clare Johnson has kept a diaristic sticky note drawing practice for two decades, amassing a collection of over 6,000 drawings (and counting). Join Johnson for a talk and hands-on activities that will help you develop your own relationship to making “everyday” art. If you haven’t seen the Day-to-Day exhibition at Henry Art Gallery (I wrote about it here ), this is your sign.

Melissa Messer at Spectrum Fine Art Melissa Messer describes her practice and work as “if Rothko’s daughter were obsessed with form.” I might add Albers to the mix. Messer is a colorist whose use of hue is almost spiritual (in which case, Rothko is the correct comparison). She is also a pre-eminent figurative painter, where the human body becomes an armature upon which to drape shades of deciduous greens, burnt orange, and acid gold. This is Messer’s first solo with Spectrum Fine Art ; a formal reception lands on October 8, but you can get a preview this weekend for Art + Culture Week.

September 26 Kelly Bjork: Lunacy at J. Rinehart Gallery No one in this city is as cool and talented as Kelly Bjork . Her drawings are full of intimacies and bodies, tenderness and acceptance, rendered in beautiful, illustrative precision. Her second solo exhibition at J. Rinehart Gallery , Lunacy , addresses queerness in a time of queer discrimination and violence. The exhibition preview opens today, 1–3 pm.

IMMINENT MODE at ArtLove Salon The seventh iteration of IMMINENT MODE , held at ArtLove Salon , brings collaborations by six teams of garment designers paired with visual artists to tell stories through wearable art and installation on the runway. This year’s artists include Anouk Rawkson, Jordan Christianson, Shiloh Davies, Shari Noble, Brandon Vosika, Jersey Virago, Dez’Mon Fair, Mariel Andrade, Devon Yan, Ruben David Rodriguez, and Debora Spencer.

articles.title: Charlie’s Queer Books Is Opening a Second Location
articles.author: Katie Lee Ellison
paras: This is the best books news I’ve heard since Roxane Gay and Debbie Millman bought The Rumpus : Charlie’s Queer Books is opening a new location in Seattle’s original gayborhood, Capitol Hill. Next door to Unicorn Bar, across the street from Wildrose, and around the corner from Elliott Bay Book Company, this new space is set to open in November.

The new store will be ADA accessible and twice as big as the Fremont location, with an events and gathering space with room for 50 seats, as well as a coffee shop and wine bar. I spoke with the owners, Charlie Hunts and Madeline Burchard, about how it all came to be.

How did you get to a place where you could open a second location? Hunts: It has been remarkable how the Seattle queer and literary community have rallied around us. At this point, we’ve run out of space. Not only on the shelves, but also in terms of what this [current] location can handle for events and as a gathering space.

The property managers of this new location are an older couple from 12th & Pike St. Associates. They understand not only what we’re doing, but why it’s important for the neighborhood. If you keep the rent at a manageable price, even if it’s still high, you can keep the businesses that make the neighborhood what it is and encourage the vitality of that space.

How important are exclusively queer bookstores these days? Burchard: Because we’re in a cross section of record book bans and anti-LGBT legislation, our bookstore holds more responsibility than the average small business. That is in the forefront of our minds every single day we open the door. It’s been touching, the way people look to us to be leaders in the community, especially when something happens that affects the community.

Do you feel ready and able for that responsibility? Burchard: Charlie and I have training for it, but it’s heavy to be like, “Okay, we gotta say the responsible thing. I hope we’re getting this right.” We won’t always, but I hope we can show up for people in the best way. Sometimes it’s tough for me to figure out our next step—what we say, what we do, or if people even want to hear from us about it. But we have a lot of young trans customers who look up to Charlie in particular. So Charlie’s is more than a third space. This is part of our social fabric.

Hunts: We also do things like watch parties and video nights. Events that are kind of stupid, silly, but essential. That’s one of our niches—to not take ourselves too seriously, to be joyful, and in touch with culture, too. We’re not just people who own a bookstore selling to gay people. We are gay people.

Do you have a vision or hopes and dreams for where this is all headed, say five years from now? Hunts: We’ve had big hand-wavy dreams, like what if this became a national thing? But it’s very hypothetical. Right now, we’re entering a new industry in coffee and food service. We’re getting a handle on that, and what’s great about this place is it allows us to support programming that doesn’t charge for tickets. So everything from a silent book club to open mic, it helps support community events and bigger authors, too.

I think our vision for the store is people come in here and they’re kind of entering into an alternate universe where they are the norm. They are the defaults. They’re not hunting the shelves for things that wreck them. They’re not in the LGBT section that’s tucked away.

Like the porn section or something. Hunts: Yes, we are always next to self-help. We have encountered bookstores where the LGBT section is next to porn, self-help. Sometimes in… a literal closet. A little closet that just didn’t have a door on it. We were like, we have to make this bookstore.

Is there anything you want to say to people about the new space? Hunts: I’m excited to keep iterating on this business, see how far we can take it, and learn as much as we can. We’re very open. Folks who came in and said, “I want to start a book club”: we let them start a book club. If folks have dreams for something, they don’t always have a space for it. We are open to these conversations. If someone is serious, they want to take charge of it, work with us, and collaborate, let’s talk about it.

articles.title: Slog AM: Robert Kraft Says He’ll Donate $2 Million to “Humanitarian Aid” After Macklemore Pledges $1 million to Palestine, Downtown Seattle Is Booming, Federal Reserve Increases the Cost of Borrowing
articles.author: Charles Mudede
paras: The average price a worker pays to commute in the Seattle area? $10,018 a year, according to a study by Consumer Affairs . And the amount of time a worker spends driving to and from a job? An hour, which is “roughly 10 full days spent [in a car annually].” Altogether, only four metropolitan areas are above ours when it comes to bleeding through the nose to get around. Automobile freedom not only doesn’t exist, it’s not cheap.

But how is the new bus lane on Denny Way going? Over the past two weeks, I’ve taken the 8 bus 10 times during rush hour, and not a single bus was late. None. Not only that, traffic jams appear to have vanished from this part of Denny Way. Where did they go? What kind of sorcery is this? Losing a lane has actually loosened rush-hour traffic? Maybe I’m just seeing things. Time will tell.

It rained on Sunday. And it was almost like real rain, the kind of rain that falls for days and makes this region dark and green like the forests in the Twilight movies. But the rain on Sunday departed around noon and, so far, refuses to return. What a tease. Today will be mostly clear and sunny. Expect a high of 75.

U.S. Rep. Marie Gluesenkamp Perez does it again. She voted with Republicans on a measure that advanced their priorities. She was one of two defections on this matter. If both “Democrats” had voted against the measure, it would have failed . The problem is this: The GOP is no longer a party. It’s just Trump. So, if you support a Republican measure, you are only supporting Trump and his massive anti-democratic project. Perez is not a centrist, as the Seattle Times keeps calling her. There is nothing like a center in US politics today.You are with Trump or you are not. It’s that simple, Perez.

Downtown Seattle is once again far from dying . It is in fact thriving. Last month, this part of town, with its waterfront, its markets, hotels, galleries, stadiums, and Link stations experienced 9.2 million visits . This is, according to data collected by an organization that has it in for Mayor Katie Willson , the Downtown Seattle Association , the busiest the downtown has been since July 2019. The DSA also reported that consumers spent an estimated $165 million in July.

Well, Trump did not get his wish —cheap cash—from the very man he placed at the top of the Federal Reserve, Kevin Warsh. Yesterday, he raised interest rates “for the first time in more than three years” because inflation is a real thing; something, anything has to be done to cool it. Rates went up by 25 basis points and are now in the 3.75 percent–4 percent range. The inflation Warsh is now battling by raising the cost of borrowing was entirely caused by Trump’s war and tariffs.

Black holes not only consume everything in sight but also expel large amounts of gas. Astronomers at the University of Florence verified this phenomenon while observing a black hole at the center of a galaxy, NGC 1066 (also called the Squid Galaxy), which is 45 million light-years from us. This black hole is a monster. It’s between “8 million and 17 million solar masses,” and it ejects much more gas than scientists expected. (This extra gas is hard to detect because it is dust poor.) But get this: The astronomers also “checked whether this gas could ever fall back toward the black hole. Comparing the outflow’s speed with the galaxy’s escape velocity, they found the gas is moving several times faster than needed to escape entirely.” The mystery of black holes only knows how to grow.

Let’s picture this. Some physicists believe, understandably, that the universe is actually the interior of a black hole. But how to make sense of this hypothesis? For one, it means the beginning is a singularity, the collapse of a dead star, and we are not moving toward it but bouncing from it. This means that in fact we are moving back in time. What we feel to be the past is actually in the future; and the past, where the singularity is located, is actually moving forward in time. This explains the nature of memory and computation. It is the future from which we are receding. And the actual past is the event horizon, which, as we approach, appears to be expanding at an accelerating rate. We call this acceleration toward the black hole’s past dark energy.

Macklemore keeps winning his war with Robert Kraft , the billionaire who forced Ed Sheeran, a coward whose music is to my ears what a wet stone is to my mouth, to drop the Seattle rapper from his Loop Tour. Macklemore challenged Kraft to match his $1 million pledge directly to Palestinian organizations, and, according to NYT , Kraft pledged $2 million to “the region.” Make of that what you will.

Linton Kwesi Johnson (also known as LKJ) is a dub poet. Dub is an abstract form of reggae, and in the late ’70s, Jamaican poets like Prince Far I and Mutabaruka used the echoing and reverberating dub rhythms as backdrops to their politically charged poems. LKJ was born in Jamaica, raised in the United Kingdom, educated as a sociologist, and was once a member of the British chapter of the Black Panther party. He used the dub-poem form to address the social and political realities of Britain’s depressed inner cities, particularly during the Thatcher years.

LKJ read (and still reads) his poetry with a thick and sometimes impenetrable Jamaican accent. For example, on “Reggae Fi Dada” (Making History, 1984), he opens with these lines: “Galang dada, galang gwwaan yaw sah/yu nevvah ad noh life fi live/jus di wan life fi give/yu did yu time pan ert/yu nevvah get yu jus dizert” (translation: “Go on daddy, go on, go on sir/you never had no life to live/just the one life to give/you did your time upon the earth/you never got your just dessert”). Some of LKJ’s dub poems surrender all meaning to the hypnotic pulse of the reggae rhythm, such as the title track of the 1978 album Dread Beat an’ Blood , which moves to a slow and bouncy reggae beat.

Today is your last chance to see the documentary about LKJ, Dread Beat an’ Blood , at the theater that won this year’s Genius Award for film, the Beacon Cinema . Because I can’t say enough about LKJ, let’s conclude AM with his masterpiece, and atheist anthem (yes, this enlightened dread does not believe in Jah), “ Reality Poem .”

articles.title: Oregon Lawmakers Seek to Open Up Affordable Housing Records Following ProPublica’s Reporting
articles.author: Rob Davis
paras: Two Oregon lawmakers want to end an unusual exemption in the state’s records law that has kept the public from learning how hundreds of millions of dollars in taxpayer money is spent on subsidized housing — and the effort has already landed key industry support.

Rep. Pam Marsh, chair of Oregon’s House Committee on Housing and Homelessness, told ProPublica that she plans to introduce legislation next year to eliminate a law that shields key details of state spending on low-income housing .

The southern Oregon Democrat said she didn’t realize the documents were being kept secret until reading about it in a ProPublica story. She said previous leaders of her committee told her they were also unaware.
“I think this is an issue that will have very broad interest,” Marsh said.
State Sen. Khanh Pham, a Portland Democrat and chair of the Senate Committee on Housing and Development, said she also wants the Legislature to tackle the issue in its next session.

Meanwhile, a lobbying group for low-income housing developers, lenders and related businesses, Housing Oregon, said it strongly supports repealing the secrecy provision; the organization has asked the state to disclose more about projects that it funds in the meantime.

“Oregon’s affordable housing providers share the public’s interest in ensuring that public investments in housing are used effectively, responsibly, and with visibility,” said Kevin Cronin, a spokesperson for the group. “The questions raised in your recent ProPublica article regarding development costs deserve serious attention.”
Cronin said Oregon can increase transparency around development costs “while still protecting genuinely proprietary or competitively sensitive information.”
“More consistent reporting of costs and outcomes will help policymakers, providers, researchers, and the public understand where the system is working and where it needs improvement,” Cronin said.

ProPublica highlighted Oregon’s secrecy around low-income housing in August. Since 2021, our story noted, Oregon has given developers an unprecedented $1.4 billion, and the cost of developing each low-income apartment has nearly doubled, to $540,000. Dozens of projects are lined up for another $850 million in future state funding, and costs are expected to continue rising.

“We are spending, as you said, a lot of money on the development of affordable housing,” Marsh said. “We really need to understand what it is that we’re funding, how much it costs, why it costs that much, and be able to justify the investments that we’re making.”
In other states, researchers and journalists have used the financial records from subsidized housing projects to investigate their spiraling costs and the drivers behind the growing price tag.

Marsh said after reading the ProPublica story that she “pretty much immediately” looked up the provision in Oregon public records law that officials cite for keeping cost details secret. She said financial documents that show where a project’s money is coming from and what it’s going to should be public and easily accessed. She said she would like to see them posted online as part of the public materials that Oregon’s Housing Stability Council receives for each project before awarding subsidies.

Pham, in a written statement, said: “It’s imperative that Oregonians can trust that our state government is investing in affordable housing as cost-effectively as possible. I appreciated ProPublica’s reporting on Oregon’s inadequate public records law that hinders our ability to monitor how affordable housing funds are being spent, and I’m hopeful legislators can address this next year.”

Oregon’s Sunshine Committee, which reviews public records exemptions and recommends ones that could be rolled back, is also examining the exemption for housing financials as a result of ProPublica’s coverage, co-chair Charlie Fisher said.

It’s not clear where opposition to repeal efforts, if any, might arise. Officials in Washington and California, where the details of state spending on subsidized housing are available to the public, have said it hasn’t interfered with low-income housing efforts.

Oregon Housing and Community Services, the state housing agency that persuaded lawmakers to create the records exemption in 1997, cited the law in redacting major sections of developers’ cost reports that ProPublica requested in May.
The agency’s current executive director, Andrea Bell, told ProPublica in July that she is committed to transparency but that the agency is following the law as it stands today.

Asked to comment this week about whether the agency would support efforts to change the law, a spokesperson said by email that state agencies don’t take positions on bills. “OHCS appreciates the opportunity to review the legislation” that’s introduced in 2027, the spokesperson wrote.
