articles.title: Foster Resurrects Housing Accelerator, Teeing Up MHA Fee Break in 2027
articles.author: Doug Trumm
paras: Seattle is taking another stab at a "Housing Accelerator" pilot program that would offer a temporary reduction on builder fees to stimulate housing starts. Councilmember Dionne Foster dropped the proposal today, which will be formally introduced Friday in the housing committee, which she chairs.

The housing accelerator idea surfaced earlier this year, with a coalition of builders called the Seattle Housing Roundtable forming to advocate for the idea . Behind the scenes, Mayor Katie Wilson backed the proposal and was preparing to release legislation when a key coalition representing nonprofit affordable housing developers pulled their support , leading the mayor to table the proposal for more stakeholder work.
The Urbanist's Fall Member Drive is in full swing! Support our work, read ad-free, and help us hit our goal for the member drive!

That process snag led some observers to worry the proposal would be trapped in the Seattle Process never to be seen again, or to be watered down past the point of usefulness. Foster's proposal seems to prove those doubts unfounded, though the delay will have an impact on how quickly the proposal can get signed into law. Due to the council budget process, which kicks off next week, the bill isn't expected to see a final vote until January.

"I'm expecting a lot of support for this proposal when we discuss it in committee on Friday," Foster told The Urbanist . "I think that we've had some really fantastic conversations with stakeholders over the last several weeks, and talked through the proposal and continue to develop the proposal in a way that I feel confident that there will be a broad support for it."

One key policy attribute remains: a 80% reduction in Mandatory Housing Affordability (MHA) fees for projects that have vested permits but are stuck in financing limbo. The Seattle Housing Roundtable has identified 35 projects encompassing more than 6,000 housing units that have vested permits, but are stuck and apparently unable to secure financing without a jolt the accelerator program could offer.

"This is really a key approach for jumpstarting housing production here in Seattle," Foster said. "We are taking this on with the goal of ensuring that housing can realistically get started in construction. So I expect to see shovels in the ground and apartment buildings opening up for our residents."

One key change: proposals that are not yet vested will be able to unlock a 60% reduction, rather than the full 80% proposed earlier. They will also need to provide 25% of units as multi-bedroom units in order to qualify for the reduction, a new requirement that could force significant designs of projects that previously would have been ready to go straight into the development pipeline.

Foster also added a carveout in the MHA reduction for neighborhoods with high displacement risk, including Chinatown-International District, the Central District, and the Rainier Valley. However, there is an exemption if the project remains owned by a "legacy homeowner" which is achieved by stipulating that the deed has not transferred title since January 1, 2026. Two of the 35 stalled vested projects are in this carveout zone.

The two-year break on fees could be a bridge to a more permanent recalibration of the MHA program. Mayor Wilson's new housing production task force is chartered with tackling that question, among others. The hope is that the group will have policy recommendations next year with plenty of time to put together the permanent program before the temporary break expires.
In a Tuesday interview with The Urbanist , Foster said the two-bedroom stipulation was intended to address the dearth of family-sized rental housing in Seattle.

"We wanted to take that approach because it feels really important to strike a strong balance between accelerating production and also accelerating the kind of production we're hoping to see in the city," Foster said. "I'm also excited for the non-vested projects. We've heard a lot around the need for family-sized units here in Seattle. I certainly hear that a lot from friends of mine who are having families. And so, for those projects that are not yet vested, those will have a requirement that at least 25% of their units are two-bedroom units."

The vast majority of new multifamily housing built in Seattle consist of one-bedrooms and studios, since those types of units allow builders to achieve higher returns per square foot. But even one-bedroom-heavy projects are drying up in the pipeline. Overall, permit applications are down 94% from their 2020 peak, and permit completions are also down, which means less MHA revenue for the City's affordable housing trust fund.

At its 2021 height, the Mandatory Housing Affordability (MHA) program pulled in $74 million in funding for affordable housing, but as housing starts have plummeted, that figure has trended below $20 million. Seattle has only pulled in about $7 million though the first eight months of 2026, said Peter Nitze, a roundtable member and workforce housing developer with the firm Nitze-Stagen , said.

Nitze's firm is anticipating advancing a project that would benefit from the housing accelerator via the 60% break, he said, noting they generally look to keep a healthy mix of multi-bedrooms given their mission and Multifamily Tax Exemption (MFTE) incentives. MFTE already encourage builders to include at least 12% two-bedroom units to qualify for a lower percentage of reduced rent units.
While his firm is poised to use the temporary break, lowering the break from 80% to 60% of the fee while adding the multi-bedroom requirement could nudge some others out of the market, Nitze said.

"I'm not a fan of it," Nitze said of the change. "I would have been much happier with an 80%. The theory here is that because unvested projects haven't even submitted the package for permit approval, that they can tweak the planning to make up for that lost 20%, and it could still make a difference. So, in theory, I think that's correct, but obviously, I would prefer... you know, the original plan was doing a 90% reduction in the first year."

Generally, though, Nitze and the housing roundtable writ large is welcoming the revised proposal as a significant improvement over the status quo, which is trending toward fewer and fewer housing starts.

"The problem is we're running out of time, and it takes years for these projects, even once they're permitted, to get out of the ground," Nitze said. "And so we're going to have a pretty significant trough in terms of delivering new rental units. So there is urgency here, and so I appreciate the council moving quickly to do it."

Alongside the temporary MHA recalibration, Foster also introduced a resolution that requests a proposal to expand MHA to Neighborhood Residential (NR) zones, formerly known as single family zones), which are currently exempt. That idea had previously been considered under former Mayor Bruce Harrell, but ultimately it did not move forward, despite significant advocacy from councilmembers like Cathy Moore , who resigned last year.

"The Council requests that Central Staff: Develop legislation implementing an inclusionary requirement for new market rate residential development in Neighborhood Residential zones for referral to the Housing, Arts and Civil Rights Committee," the resolution states.
The move appears geared to win some support from stakeholders on the nonprofit side , some of whom see the lack of MHA in NR zones as an oversight sapping revenue.

Townhome builders have criticized efforts to expand MHA into NR zones, noting the margins are smaller on their project and their access to capital is more limited than builders of large apartment buildings and condominiums.

"It's certainly not going to help with making single-family homes more affordable," Nitze said. "Expanding MHA to include single family, I don't see how that's helpful. It sort of dilutes the main intent here. The main intent is to get 35 projects out of the ground by getting them over the line on the return profile, and build 6,700 units. And [if] you start tacking on a bunch of other stuff, that has unintended consequences.

Since Seattle levies MHA fees at the point of permit completion, that becomes a large burden for builders to carry before the project begins bringing in revenue. This timing challenge has led some builders to call for the reform of making the MHA fee due at the point the building receives an occupancy permit, rather before construction has even started.
Without the lifeboat that the housing accelerator could offer over the next two years, Nitze expects the development pipeline to dry up and rents to spike.
Foster seemed to agree the status quo is trending badly. While housing permit applications are plummeting in Seattle, the region is expected to continue to see significant population growth .

"Seattle is a majority renter city, and we need to make sure that we have new housing production to accommodate the growth that we're going to have here," Foster said. "And we're going to continue to grow as a city. We're a place that people want to live in. We're a place that is going to be a more climate resilient region. And it's really important that we are supporting the housing production to accommodate our population."

Correction : This article was updated shortly after publication to remove a reference to Nitze-Stagen's Swift project in Othello, which is in a displacement risk area carved out from the legislation and not likely to need an MHA exemption anyway given the number of affordable units planned. On September 17, the article was further updated to expand upon the displacement risk carveout.

articles.title: Seattle Breaks Ground on West Seattle RV Safe Lot
articles.author: Doug Trumm
paras: Last Thursday, the Low Income Housing Institute (LIHI) hosted a groundbreaking ceremony for Seattle's Glassyard Commons, a new RV safe lot near South Park that is intended to provide another pathway out of homelessness and into stable housing.

The facility will feature parking for 72 recreational vehicles (RVs) and 20 tiny houses on 3.9-acre site that LIHI is leasing from the Washington State Department of Transportation (WSDOT). The triangular parcel is hemmed in by 2nd Avenue SW and W Marginal Way SW and located just south of the 1st Avenue S bridge over the Duwamish River. LIHI expects Glassyard Commons to open by mid-November and serve 140 people.

The WSDOT property had been considered as a site for transitional housing during a previous mayoral administration , according to reporting from the West Seattle Blog, but ultimately moved forward quickly after Katie Wilson took office promising to add 1,000 shelter beds within her first year in office. This week, Wilson scaled back that plan to a more achievable 1,000 beds by the end of 2027 .
The Urbanist's Fall Member Drive is in full swing! Support our work, read ad-free, and help us hit our goal for the member drive!

At the groundbreaking, LIHI Executive Director Sharon Lee emphasized that the lot is intended to serve people who are homeless – and that surrendering their vehicle once they're permanently housed is part of the bargain.

"There could be as many as 300, 400 RVs [across Seattle]," Lee said. "Not all of them will want to come into the safe lot because part of the requirement for the safe lot is that they consider moving into housing. Not that they, you know, just hang out here, right? This is not just a parking place for people traveling through Seattle. This is for people who have no home except to survive in a RV, and oftentimes the RVs are pretty derelict, rundown, and unsafe."

Lee said these rundown RVs pose a public health risk. Councilmember Dan Strauss, who was not at the event, has also raised the issue and proposed legislation ramping up enforcement on illegally parked RVs, including seizure of non-compliant vehicles. In order to be admitted to the safe lot, RVs will be drained of fuel and electrified, with the ultimate goal of transitioning its residents into a different form of housing.

“People die living in dilapidated RVs because they are dangerous and can catch on fire. Far too many people are trying to survive in RVs because they don’t have access to housing they can afford," Lee said. "Glassyard Commons will create pathways to stable housing and will help remove hundreds of RVs off the streets of Seattle.”

As of last week, the site consisted largely of gravel and markers showing where structures will be placed. Construction has already begun on a concrete pad for a shared kitchen and utilities for the RV spaces, Lee said.
The City of Seattle, through the Human Services Department (HSD), will be providing $3.3 million in annual funding to support operations on site.

“My top priority is getting people inside with quality shelter and access to services," Mayor Katie Wilson said in a statement. "Every person experiencing homelessness has their own unique hurdles we need to help them overcome, and it is important to provide a range of types of shelter and services. Glassyard Commons will provide a personalized approach for individuals living in unsafe and unhealthy RVs, giving them a path to the help they need and permanent housing.”

Glassyard Commons will feature a staffed entry pavilion, 24/7 staff, case management offices, a community kitchen, and hygiene and laundry facilities, LIHI said. "On-site case managers will support participants with obtaining identification, employment, health and behavioral health services, education, and housing navigation."

Councilmember Bob Kettle (District 7) stressed that RV lots fit well into a public safety response. During a recent City Council meeting, Kettle claimed that unsupervised pods of RVs often become magnets for illegal activity, like drug dealing and trafficking in stolen goods. Kettle has become one of the mayor's biggest critics in recent weeks, particularly when it comes to issues surrounding the Seattle Police Department, but in this case aligned himself fairly directly with Wilson's overall goals for increasing shelter capacity.
“When we have a big collection of RVs, oftentimes one starts dealing drugs and we have a drug market,” Kettle said. “And once you have a drug market, you have a stolen goods market.”
At the ceremony, Kettle noted his advocacy for the Salmon Bay Village , a former RV safe lot in Interbay, which provided a template on which Glassyard Commons was modeled.

"I saw it very directly before I became a councilmember, as someone in the community that was engaged," Kettle said. "I was working this really hard in terms of the Salmon Bay Village project, and I saw how it worked. I saw the work that LIHI put in in terms of community outreach, for example, with the Magnolia Community Council and other groups, but then also implementing the lessons learned [...] having the counselor there to work with the people to break that emotional link between the RV, and then moving on to housing. That is so key."
When The Urbanist asked if he supports Strauss's RV legislation, Kettle demurred, saying the package of bills had to work its way through the committee process.

"At the end of the day, we have to get to a place where we're doing right for those that are in crisis, our neighbors, but also for our neighborhoods," Kettle said. "And I'm looking for that balance, and basically looking to address the seam that exists between traditional public safety, but also the public health, housing, and services."

In its press release, LIHI has stressed that getting unsafe RVs off Seattle streets is key part of their mission: "The goal of Glassyard Commons is to encourage vehicle residents to leave their rundown RVs, move temporarily into the safe lot or a tiny house, and work with case managers to obtain permanent housing. Once housing is secured, the RVs are demolished and disposed of by LIHI at no cost to the participants. This prevents the RVs from being recirculated back onto the streets of Seattle."
Brian Nielson, WSDOT's regional administrator for Northwest Region, spoke at the event, highlighting that encampments encroaching on highway right-of-way have been an issue for the state.

"We need to be clear about transportation: It's not a safe place to live," Nielson said. "The areas are designed for highways and transportation infrastructure. Living there puts people close to traffic and other hazards. They do not provide the basic infrastructure and services that people need to live safely. This is why Glassyard Commons matters. WSDOT is providing the property, but LIHI and their partners are creating something much more important: a place where people have safety and stability, access to services and case management, and the opportunity to work toward permanent housing. This is what partnership should look like."

The auditory experience of the groundbreaking made clear that while the safe lot won't be located directly on highway right-of-way, it's still sandwiched into a busy trucking corridor with plenty of loud traffic going by. Amenities are scant in the industrial area, although the nautically themed Mighty Mugs Coffee Shop and a truck stop Subway sandwich shop are about a 10-minute walk away. The lot is close to a bus stop.

LIHI had been working with WSDOT for a long time to find surplus land that could work for a project, Lee said. Given the large amount of space they need and the potential for complaints from neighbors, RV safe lots have largely been sited in industrial areas.

Referrals for spots at Glassyard will be made from outreach workers contracted through the HSD. Preference will be given to Council District 1 and other locations with large numbers of RVs, LIHI noted.
HSD Director Tanya Kim noted that more shelter expansions and tiny home villages were on the way.

"The City is investing in two more tiny home villages, a master leased shelter, and two shelter expansions that are scheduled to open at the end of this year and at the beginning of next year," Kim said. "So there is much more coming, and they're diversified."

To accelerate permitting for the RV safe lot, LIHI partnered with New Hope Missionary Baptist Church, allowing it to benefit for an incentive program reducing red tape. The New Hope Missionary Baptist Church was also the faith sponsor of Salmon Bay Village, which Reverend Dr. Robert Jeffrey Sr. noted was a success in a statement.

“Glassyard Commons is a proven concept offering safe RV parking and is modeled after the success of Salmon Bay Village RV Safe Lot in Interbay," Jeffrey said. "Over a short period of time 67 RVs were taken off city streets and destroyed and 89 people, including five homeless veterans, received services, shelter or housing to exit homelessness.”
On Thursday, a New Hope church member named Erica also delivered the clearest call to action of the program, urging Seattle to invest even more in the social safety net to lift more out of poverty.

"Dr. Martin Luther King says any religion that professes to be concerned about the souls of men, humans, and not concerned about the slums that damn them, the economic conditions that strangle them, and the social conditions that cripple them is a spiritually morbid religion awaiting burial," Erica said. "And so today, as I stand here as a faith representative for New Hope Church, it's good to be here. I see this as a glass full, but we must be reminded in this place today that this is not just the only thing that we must do. We must continue to fight for the liberation and well-being of all people."

articles.title: Bellevue Council Faces Decision Point on Parking Reform
articles.author: Ryan Packer
paras: The Eastside's largest city is grappling with a new state mandate to scale back its off-street parking requirements for new development. In facing choices around going further than the new state-required baseline, Bellevue's leaders are facing crosswinds: a desire to continue reducing barriers to homebuilding is crashing into the city's car-oriented status quo.
The Urbanist's Fall Member Drive is in full swing! Support our work, read ad-free, and help us hit our goal for the member drive!

The new mandate is coming thanks to Senate Bill 5184 , a law approved last year that sets strict caps on the number of off-street parking stalls that Washington cities can require with new building projects. By next January, Bellevue will no longer be able to require more than one parking stall for every two apartment units, nor more than two parking stalls for every 1,000 square feet of commercial space.

The City will also be barred from requiring any parking for a broad set of uses, including apartments less than 1,200 square feet in size, commercial spaces that are less than 3,000 square feet, child care facilities, and affordable and senior housing.

The statewide parking reform is intended to ease cost burdens on builders, which are passed along to renters and homebuyers. Adding garage parking typically costs builders $60,000 per stall or more, according to the housing-focused Pacific Northwest think tank Sightline Institute.

Cities across the state are grappling with the new requirements, but Bellevue's size, prevalence of transit infrastructure, and positive trends in housing permit starts are putting a spotlight on how this new mandate gets implemented. Earlier this year, numerous councilmembers expressed clear interest in looking at how to be more ambitious in giving developers flexibility around parking, but recommendations that came out of Bellevue's planning commission hew much closer to the bare minimum.

A growing number of Washington cities are taking steps to fully eliminate parking mandates from their land use codes, following in the footsteps of places like Spokane , Port Townsend , and Bellingham . Vancouver abolished parking mandates as part of its Comprehensive Plan update earlier this year, with Tacoma next on deck. Next door to Bellevue in Issaquah, city leaders are considering eliminating mandates across a wide swath of the center city – an area where increasing housing growth is the goal.

A full repeal is likely a step too far for Bellevue, no matter the studies showing the range of positive benefits that come from doing so. Earlier this year, UCLA's Institute of Transportation Studies published a new research synthesis looking at a range of studies considering the impact of arbitrary requirements to build parking and the quantified benefits that come from wiping them off the books.

"Across the research literature, scholars generally recommend eliminating minimum parking requirements. Removing these mandates lifts a major barrier to new housing and businesses, reduces the risk of parking oversupply, and encourages more efficient use of existing spaces," the researchers noted. "Slowing the growth of parking infrastructure can improve walkability and urban design, reduce environmental harms, and support more sustainable travel behavior."
A full repeal is likely a step too far for Bellevue officials, so instead the debate will focus on pulling a few additional levers.

"Considering that we have appropriately aggressive housing goals, and that many projects are struggling to move forward, I think we should continue to keep our foot on the gas. And I think there are some modifications we should consider to the final code, so that we can do that," Bellevue Deputy Mayor Dave Hamilton said last week.

By 2029, Bellevue will need to remove parking mandates from within a half-mile walk of light rail stations and within a quarter-mile of RapidRide bus stops. The city is going ahead and making that update now, but the council could expand that radius to a half-mile distance from RapidRide stations, which includes the B Line and the K Line , planned to open by 2030.

"Council has already established policy direction that we want more housing capacity near high-capacity transit, including allowing six units by right in a half mile of light rail and quarter mile of bus rapid transit [BRT], removing mandatory parking requirements in those areas that are transit served is consistent with the broader direction," Councilmember Vishal Bhargava said. "I would ask that we consider [...] the half mile around the BRT, and just as an analysis to see what the puts and takes would be towards that."
Naren Briar was the only councilmember to bring up the idea of a full repeal of parking mandates, laying down a potential marker for the future.

"I am personally interested in exploring citywide elimination of parking minimums. According to the research I did, cities like Austin, San Jose, Buffalo, had done this and seen a tremendous amount of economic boost as a result of that. So I do want us to, to be clear, I think if we did that now, it might cause a little bit of chaos," Briar said. "But I do want us eventually to see a city that is comprehensively integrated and allows end-to-end walkability as an effective mode of transportation for senior citizens, for young kids waiting at the bus stop, for for any resident or visitor of Bellevue."

Another issue likely to come up before a final vote in October is visitor parking. The draft code approved by the planning commission includes a set of requirements on top of the minimum required parking stalls for residential units, mandating every development with more than six units include one visitor stall for every 20 units. After 50 units or 20,000 square feet of gross floor area that requirement no longer applies, bizarrely.

"I'm inclined to think that our mandate should be eliminated, and I'm looking to Seattle and Redmond, where they don't have any visitor parking mandate," Hamilton said. "I think housing providers understand their customers' preferences and will build projects accordingly. This may be an area where we can follow the lead of neighboring cities and help ensure that folks who move here are not penalized."

There will also be a push in the other direction. At last Tuesday's meeting, a clear bloc formed in favor of sticking with the planning commission recommendation that included Jared Nieuwenhuis, Lynne Robinson, and Claire Sumadiwirya.

"Myself, I live in a townhouse community, so I would say if there's no visitor parking, somebody is not able to walk a half mile, take the light rail, then nobody's gonna ever visit me," Sumadiwirya said. "I have a lot of elderly friends, so I think it's really important to know that. I appreciate the take of meet the state minimum first. I think whenever there's something [that] changes in the policy, it's always good to be safe and finding that balance versus just I think making drastic, too bold changes that will be different."

Robinson, who served as Bellevue's mayor from 2020 to 2025, went even further than her colleagues and suggested that the city might make a push to amend state law to mandate parking at senior living facilities. She pushed back most strenuously on the idea of going further than the planning commission recommendation.

"Nobody's going to have service providers serve the seniors. Nobody's going to get a visitor, and Silver Glen is our only, I think, our only independent [living facility]," Robinson said. "I guess there's one next to Emerald Court, but independent senior living, and all those people have cars, and most of them cannot walk that far, so they're staying connected to the community by having the ability to drive, and if we take the parking away, it's going to really limit people's ability to live independently."

According to the National Resources Defense Council , 37.6% of Americans over the age of 75 have driving limitations, as of 2025. Nothing in the land use code would limit the ability for developers of senior and independent living facilities from building off-street parking with their projects – removing the mandate simply gets the city out of the business of deciding what's appropriate.
While not likely to represent a major sea change, the October 20 vote on parking reform will certainly signal what direction Bellevue is heading.

articles.title: “Hop On Board!” Campaign Kicks Off
articles.author: Nathan Dickey
paras: Yesterday, a coalition of transit advocates launched “Hop On Board!”, the official campaign urging Seattle voters to pass the renewal and expansion of the Seattle Transit Measure this November . Speakers at the event included Seattle Mayor Katie Wilson, Councilmember Alexis Mercedes Rinck, ATU 587 President Greg Woodfill, Nondrivers Alliance founder Anna Zivarts, Transit Riders Union General Manager Lam Ho, and Transportation Choices Coalition ‘s Executive Director Kirk Hovenkotter and Policy Director Katy Ricchiuto.

The Transportation Choices Coalition is leading local advocates pushing for expansion of the transit measure, which proposes to increase the current 0.15% sales tax for transit to 0.3%, the maximum allowed under recently adopted state law. If approved by voters, the measure would take effect in April 2027.

King County Metro uses an equity framework to distribute service across King County but cities have the ability to purchase additional service. Seattle has been buying additional service since 2014 , which brought frequent buses to most of the city and dramatically increased the viability of living car-free.

The current Seattle Transit Measure funds over 7% of all bus trips currently running in Seattle, mainly boosting service along key corridors during the day and providing the majority of Metro’s Night Owl service in the city. The expanded STM would further boost service at night and on weekends, as well as more than doubling the number of free ORCA cards for those who need it and providing funding for several important accessibility programs. The measure also includes funding for capital funding for bus lanes.

At the event, speakers shared stories of how important transit is to their lives and how this measure would make public transit in Seattle more useful for more people. Mayor Wilson focused on the importance of late night bus service to help service workers get home at the end of a late shift without using a rideshare service like Uber or Lyft, or making it possible for a family with two cars to only need one.

Councilmember Rinck shared stories of three-seat rides to Tumwater and the importance of frequent, reliable service, and also highlighted the expanded late night service provided by the measure. Greg Woodfill posited that although sales taxes are regressive, this measure’s taxes will go right back to serving the people who need it most, stating “every $1 spent on transit is $5 back in the community”. Anna Zivarts stressed the importantance of frequent and reliable service to those who cannot drive, and how the transit measure would bring more service to more communities. Zivarts put it simply: “transit is freedom”. Other speakers highlighted the proposed increase in free ORCA passes for low-income riders and the elderly, and the importance of pushing back against likely opposition to the measure.
If you are intersested in supporting the Hop On Board campaign, you can sign up to volunteer for upcoming events , or donate to the campaign .

articles.title: Cafe Lolo Is the Neighborhood Restaurant Every Neighborhood Deserves
articles.author: <name>Kat Thompson</name>
paras: If I were to describe the perfect neighborhood restaurant, Cafe Lolo would completely fit my definition. The food is comforting and nourishing, emphasizing local ingredients, which playfully come together in a way that feels both fresh and familiar. The space is draped in natural light that’s assisted by over a dozen lamps. The inviting dining room is covered in quirky Renaissance-inspired murals that don’t feel disruptive. There are to-go meal kits available for purchase, as well as local beers. It’s an atmosphere that invites you to unwind with a bottle of wine. Owners Leah Engel, Alex Halmi, and Brett Bankson are present, not only flitting about the room, but also cooking the dishes in the kitchen and laughing with customers. If I lived in the neighborhood, just off the main drag of Capitol Hill, it’s somewhere I’d want to return to over and over again.

Cafe Lolo has an extensive wine menu and many local beers, as well as bottles in the fridge you can pick up to-go. Although yes, the wine list — which includes just one glass from Washington, and more options from Oregon and Europe) — is worth perusing, the nonalcoholic tisanes are also made from seasonal ingredients. The strawberry rhubarb soda I had on my visit was effervescent and floral without an overpowering sweetness.

Like the rest of the menu, dessert will change pending seasons — but don’t skip it. My visit included a celebration of ripe, macerated strawberries over a semolina olive oil cake, which had a buttery crust and a tender interior crumb. There was also a scoop of rhubarb sorbet; light, sweet, and sharp.
